text: Use named exports for JavaScript/TypeScript modules rather than default exports. React components under `client/src/components/` are the exception: export the main component with `export default ComponentName;` at the end of the file. When editing existing modules, preserve existing named exports and class names — do not convert a named export to a default or anonymous export without updating all import sites.
reason: Named exports improve discoverability, keep import names consistent, and are refactor-safe; the React-component default export is a narrow, documented exception. Silently changing a named export to a default breaks other modules that import it and can cause runtime failures.
scope: JavaScript/TypeScript modules; React components in `client/src/components/` use default export
common_pattern: JavaScript/TypeScript module import/export conventions: prefer named exports, consolidate imports, choose the correct import form for libraries (React namespace import), and keep barrel files minimal and consistent — while preserving existing export names to avoid breaking consumers.

text: In barrel/index files (e.g. `client/src/index.ts`), expose modules using direct re-exports (`export { name } from './module'`) applied consistently to every entry. When a module's entire export is a single existing object/const, export it directly (`module.exports = identifiers`) instead of spreading into a new object. Do not create a barrel that only aggregates imports/exports for a single consumer — define the mapping directly in the importing file.
reason: Direct re-exports keep barrel files concise and their public API easy to scan; exporting a single value directly avoids an unnecessary shallow copy and preserves object identity; avoiding single-consumer barrels removes pointless indirection.
scope: barrel/entry files such as `client/src/index.ts` and module export statements
common_pattern: JavaScript/TypeScript module import/export conventions: prefer named exports, consolidate imports, choose the correct import form for libraries (React namespace import), and keep barrel files minimal and consistent — while preserving existing export names to avoid breaking consumers.

text: In `wagtail/models/__init__.py`, re-export `WorkflowManager` so it remains importable from `wagtail.models`, preserving the existing public API for downstream projects that subclass it for custom `AbstractWorkflow` implementations.
reason: This avoids breaking external code that previously imported or subclassed `WorkflowManager` from `wagtail.models`; removing the re-export would be an unintended API regression.
common_pattern: Wagtail model API/class conventions, with two distinct sub-patterns: preserving public re-exports from `wagtail.models` and maintaining canonical mixin ordering for model classes.

text: When transition constants are no longer referenced, remove them from both the JS export (e.g., `Transition.js`) and the matching SCSS file (e.g., `Transition.scss`) to keep exports and styles in sync.
reason: Avoids dead code and prevents stale or misleading APIs from accumulating.
common_pattern: SCSS/CSS transition and animation conventions: use project transition abstractions, specify explicit/performant properties, share timing values, avoid transform conflicts, and clean up unused transition constants.

text: Public block validation error classes should be included in the module's `__all__` so they can be imported from the package namespace (e.g. `wagtail.blocks`), consistent with existing exports like StreamBlockValidationError and ListBlockValidationError.
reason: Maintains a consistent public API and makes validation errors importable from the expected package location.
common_pattern: Design conventions for custom block-validation ValidationError subclasses in Wagtail: how their error groups are exposed, how their constructors default internal fields, whether they are publicly exported, and when they should exist at all.

text: When refactoring slug/URLify behavior, keep existing template/JS compatibility globals (e.g. `window.unicodeSlugsEnabled`) in place until the replacement implementation is complete and all dependent code has been migrated; defer removal of these compatibility variables to follow-up work.
reason: Removing the compatibility global early breaks existing editor behavior that still depends on it.
scope: Wagtail admin editor JS/template compatibility variables
common_pattern: Maintaining correct slug/URLify generation behavior in Wagtail — both the URLify API contract and the behavioral parity of the replacement implementation — while the urlify.js migration is in progress.

text: Do not prune LogEntry fields such as `content_changed` and `deleted` while they are still required for filtering; defer their removal until the planned inheritance-based action hierarchy makes them redundant.
reason: These fields serve ongoing filtering needs, and the future inheritance-based action hierarchy that would make them redundant is not yet implemented.
common_pattern: Audit-log / LogEntry correctness: log entries must remain accurate and unambiguous for their consumers — fields kept only as long as they're needed for filtering, values captured before destructive operations, and messages worded without time-relative qualifiers.

text: When moving a built-in panel out of the user-defined panels tree and hard-coding it into the view, give the hard-coded implementation a new class name and keep the legacy panel class as an always-hidden no-op rather than deleting it, so existing user references to the old class do not cause duplicate definitions or rendering.
reason: Preserves backwards compatibility for users who still reference the old panel class while preventing duplicate panel definitions or rendering after the built-in panel is hard-coded into the view.
common_pattern: Backwards-compatible migration of built-in panels out of the user-defined panels tree by renaming the new hard-coded implementation and neutralising the legacy panel class instead of deleting it.

text: When a utility or helper is marked for removal (e.g. by a TODO stating it should be replaced by an existing object property), do not extend it with new functionality; implement or verify the intended replacement instead.
reason: Investing in code maintainers have already marked for deletion wastes effort and diverges from the original design intent.
common_pattern: Helper/wrapper hygiene: minimize redundant computation and unnecessary indirection around helper functions — reuse the results and encapsulation of existing helpers instead of re-calling or duplicating their logic, and avoid creating new single-use wrapper helpers that only delegate to an existing call.

text: When a notification flow is replaced (e.g., by a notifier class with new templates) or an admin URL route is deleted, remove the obsolete mail helper functions from `wagtail/admin/mail.py` and update or delete the corresponding notification templates under `wagtailadmin/notifications/` — including any that reference the removed URL names.
reason: Templates and helpers referencing deleted URLs become dead code that can produce broken links or be invoked accidentally, obscuring the current notification path.
common_pattern: Both sub-patterns concern Wagtail admin notification emails: (a) which send helper to use depending on whether the email belongs to a Wagtail notification flow vs. an existing Django auth flow, and (b) cleaning up obsolete mail helpers/templates when a notification flow or URL route is removed. They share the notification-email theme but address distinct concerns (sender selection vs. dead-code cleanup).

text: In `wagtail/admin/templatetags/wagtailadmin_tags.py`, template tags that only serialize data for the `admin_base.html` initial config script should be deprecated and/or converted to plain helper functions following the `get_js_translation_strings()` pattern: return Python data and let the consumer handle JSON serialization instead of keeping `{% ... %}` indirection or embedding `json.dumps()` in the tag. If backward compatibility is needed, add a `serialize=True` parameter: emit `warnings.warn(...)` and `json.dumps(...)` on the legacy serialization path, and return the raw value when `serialize=False` so internal callers can use it as a plain function.
reason: Converges on deprecating/replacing single-use serialization template tags with plain functions, while preserving backwards compatibility via an explicit serialize flag.
scope: Wagtail admin template tags, especially helpers feeding `wagtail_config` / `admin_base.html` inline config
common_pattern: Template tags in wagtailadmin_tags.py that exist only to serialize admin config data for a single consumer should be deprecated or converted into plain helper functions returning Python data, with serialization handled by the caller, following the get_js_translation_strings() pattern.

text: Treat backwards-incompatible changes (e.g., dropping a supported Python version, breaking public APIs, requiring users to update registrations) as major-release changes: bump the package version accordingly in setup.py, and keep release metadata and `{versionadded}`/upgrade-consideration docs aligned with that major version. If no other breaking changes are planned for the next release, delay the change so breaking changes can be batched into a single major release.
reason: Major version boundaries are the only clear opt-in point for breaking changes; bundling and delaying them keeps minor releases backwards-compatible and avoids surprising users on patch/minor upgrades.
common_pattern: Semantic-versioning discipline for breaking changes: any backwards-incompatible change (including dropping a supported Python version) must land in a major release, which requires a major version bump and alignment of release metadata/directives; when no companion breaking changes exist, the change should be deferred to batch with other breaking changes rather than skipping ahead.

text: Prefer SVG icons over legacy icon fonts; treat icon fonts as deprecated and migrate remaining legacy font-family usage to a Sass variable so stylelint rules can be enabled globally instead of relying on `null` or permanent exceptions.
reason: This captures the shared deprecation/migration pattern across the icon-font generalizations: move away from legacy icon fonts and avoid permanent lint exceptions.
common_pattern: Project icon-asset conventions: reuse/reviewed icon sources and accurate attribution, plus deprecating legacy icon fonts in favor of SVG.

text: When replacing legacy telepath behavior (e.g., with BlockController), remove the superseded initialization code from the Telepath block files and add a reminder comment near any compatibility guards (e.g., `if (!window.telepath)`) indicating they can be simplified or removed once the legacy `telepath.js` module is deleted.
reason: Ensures obsolete code is cleaned up and temporary shims are documented for future removal, preventing legacy support code from lingering.
scope: telepath migration and legacy code cleanup
common_pattern: Cleanup of legacy telepath code when replaced by new block controller behavior: removing superseded initialization code and adding reminder comments for compatibility shims that depend on the legacy telepath.js module.

text: When renaming URL route names or patterns (e.g., Django/Wagtail routes), update every reverse() call and reference to the old name across the codebase, and add upgrade or release notes documenting the old -> new name mapping for every affected app or module.
reason: URL names are public API; failing to update references causes NoReverseMatch errors, and incomplete migration notes leave users without a clear upgrade path.
common_pattern: Propagating URL route name/pattern renames across code references and migration documentation

text: Avoid deprecated `KeyboardEvent.keyCode` and legacy browser-specific key aliases (e.g., legacy Edge's `Left`, `Right`); use standard `KeyboardEvent.code` (e.g., `'KeyM'`) or `KeyboardEvent.key` values (e.g., `'ArrowLeft'`, `'ArrowRight'`) instead.
reason: `keyCode` is deprecated, varies by browser and keyboard layout, and legacy aliases add dead code; standard properties are reliable and aligned with supported browsers.
common_pattern: Best practices for handling keyboard events: use modern standard properties and shared constants instead of deprecated or hard-coded values, drop legacy browser-specific aliases, and ensure accessible activation keys.

text: Remove imports that are not actually referenced in the file, including imports left unused after a refactor, imports added before their first use, and imports of symbols/components no longer used in tests or when switching away from a library. Delete them outright rather than commenting them out, since version control preserves the history. When refactoring Django code, keep surrounding module declarations consistent with the change: remove imports the change made unused (e.g. a now-unused `django.conf.settings` import after a value becomes a constant), and preserve unrelated Django declarations such as `default_app_config` in app `__init__.py` files unless you are intentionally migrating app configuration. If an import is intentionally retained for side effects or a setup-time workaround despite appearing unused, make that intent explicit with an inline comment explaining why, rather than leaving a bare unused import or relying only on a linter suppression.
reason: Unused imports are dead code: they add noise, can trigger lint/import failures, mislead readers about a module's real dependencies, and may keep unnecessary third-party libraries in the dependency graph. In Django refactors, stale imports misrepresent module dependencies, while accidentally dropping `default_app_config` breaks Django app config discovery in a way unrelated to the intended change. Documented side-effect or setup imports prevent future maintainers from removing required imports or being confused by unexplained suppressions.
common_pattern: Unused imports (including those left behind after refactors) must be removed rather than left in the codebase or commented out; exceptions for intentional side-effect imports must be documented explicitly.

text: Import React using namespace syntax (`import * as React from 'react'`) rather than `import React from 'react'`. Combine multiple imports from the same module into a single statement (e.g., `import React, { useState } from 'react';`) instead of adding duplicate import lines.
reason: The namespace import is the officially recommended form and works regardless of `esModuleInterop` settings; consolidating imports avoids duplicates and satisfies `import/no-duplicates` linting rules.
common_pattern: JavaScript/TypeScript module import/export conventions: prefer named exports, consolidate imports, choose the correct import form for libraries (React namespace import), and keep barrel files minimal and consistent — while preserving existing export names to avoid breaking consumers.

text: Do not import names that are already defined in or imported into the same module — reference them directly. When importing multiple names from the same module, use a single `from module import a, b` statement instead of repeating the `from module import` prefix on separate lines.
reason: Same-module imports are redundant, add noise, and can misleadingly imply a circular dependency or external source; combining same-module imports reduces duplication and matches common Python style conventions.
common_pattern: Python import conventions: where imports belong (module top level by default), when function-scoped imports are acceptable, how to keep imports consistent with the project's established paths, and how to avoid redundant imports.

text: When importing optional Django app models or triggering module side effects, respect Django's app-loading order: keep Django app package `__init__.py` files free of top-level imports that pull in models or model-dependent modules, do not add redundant duplicate side-effect imports in `models.py` for modules already imported by the package `__init__.py`, and guard optional app model imports against `RuntimeError` (via `apps.is_installed()` / `apps.get_model()` or catching `RuntimeError` alongside `ImportError`) because importability does not imply the app is in `INSTALLED_APPS`.
reason: Package `__init__.py` runs before any submodule and during app loading, so importing models there creates circular-import breakage; conversely, assuming a module needs an extra side-effect import ignores that its package `__init__` already loaded it. Model class creation for an uninstalled app raises `RuntimeError`, not `ImportError`, so `ImportError`-only guards fail.
common_pattern: Working correctly with Django framework internals: respecting app-loading/import ordering semantics and avoiding mutations of or reliance on Django's private/internal machinery (historical models, app_config state, defensive signal guards).

text: In a Python 3-only codebase, omit all Python 2 compatibility boilerplate: `from __future__ import unicode_literals` / `absolute_import`, `# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-` encoding declarations, and `try: import <py2 module> except ImportError:` shims. Import directly using Python 3 module paths (e.g. `from urllib.parse import urlparse, urlencode`) and remove stale `# Generated by Django 1.x` headers from migrations.
reason: Python 3 strings are Unicode by default and source files default to UTF-8, so this boilerplate is redundant, adds legacy noise, and misleadingly implies support for unsupported runtimes. (Note: an earlier phase of this project required `from __future__ import unicode_literals` for Py2/Py3 compatibility; that rule is superseded now that Python 2 support has been dropped.)
scope: global for Python source files and generated migrations
common_pattern: Python 2 compatibility boilerplate (encoding declarations, `from __future__` imports, py2 import shims) should be governed by the project's supported Python version. The cluster is temporally split: older PRs (2179, 2459, 2751) mandated adding `unicode_literals` for Py2/Py3 compatibility, while later PRs (4062, 4066, 4560, 6451, 11107) mandate removing that same boilerplate once the project became Python 3-only. These are not genuine contradictions but an evolution driven by dropping Python 2 support.

text: Preserve exact casing when working with imports: import named exports using the exact exported identifier casing, reference module paths with the exact on-disk file casing, and avoid introducing identifiers that differ from an import only by case.
reason: JavaScript imports and case-sensitive filesystems require exact casing; mismatched casing breaks resolution/builds, while case-only identifier differences are confusing and can mask reference errors.
common_pattern: Casing discipline for imports: imported bindings, module paths, and related exported/global identifiers must use exact, non-confusing casing.

text: When subclassing a class defined in another package/module, import that base class directly from its defining module and use the imported name as the base class, rather than a dotted module attribute path.
reason: Direct imports keep class declarations concise and explicit, avoid depending on an intermediate module's re-exported namespace, and make the base class easier to locate and refactor.
common_pattern: Python class-declaration hygiene: keep class headers minimal — no redundant empty parentheses or explicit `object` base when there is no base class, and reference a real base class by its directly imported name rather than a redundant syntactic form.

text: Use import aliases only when they add clarity or disambiguation (e.g., renaming a generic function like `activate` to `activate_lang`) or for an intentional re-export. Avoid redundant aliases where the alias is identical to the imported name (`import X as X` or `from module import X as X`).
reason: Redundant aliases add unnecessary noise and obscure whether the alias carries semantic meaning. Conversely, when an imported name is generic or ambiguous, an alias improves clarity at call sites.
common_pattern: Import alias usage: aliases should only be introduced when they improve clarity/disambiguation; redundant aliases that duplicate the imported name are noise.

text: Use the modern Sass module system and dependency-aware ordering for SCSS imports. Prefer `@forward`/`@use` over the deprecated `@import`; place `@use` statements at the top of the file before local module variables; omit the `.scss` extension when referencing partials (per the `scss/at-import-partial-extension-blacklist` stylelint rule); and import shared styles through configured import paths or existing non-relative conventions rather than deep relative paths like `../../../../../client/scss/...`. Order imports so widely reused shared/base partials and component styles precede dependent styles that consume or override them (e.g. `page-editor` and `buttons` before `modals`), so the cascade resolves at the source and avoids unnecessary specificity in downstream overrides.
reason: `@import` is deprecated, pollutes the global namespace, and can duplicate CSS output; `@use` placed first is idiomatic and readable; deep relative paths are brittle and make files hard to move or refactor; CSS cascade and specificity depend on import order, so correct ordering avoids override conflicts and reduces brute-force specificity fixes.
scope: SCSS files and stylesheets such as `client/scss/core.scss`, `client/scss/**/*.scss`, and `wagtail/admin/static_src/**/*.scss`
common_pattern: SCSS/Sass module and import conventions: keeping imports well-ordered, dependency-directed, and using the modern module system rather than legacy patterns.

text: Type function parameters and return values against the most general applicable type rather than a narrower concrete subtype. Use `django.core.files.File` instead of `UploadedFile` when the logic does not need subtype-specific extras, and annotate Django context-data parameters/returns as `Mapping[str, Any]` instead of `Context` or `dict`, since both satisfy the `Mapping` interface and callers may pass either.
reason: This keeps reusable utilities decoupled from a specific context, accepts any implementation of the general abstraction or mapping-like value, and preserves accurate type information for callers.
common_pattern: Both generalizations express the same API/typing principle: function parameters should use the most general applicable type instead of a narrower subtype when the implementation does not rely on subtype-specific behavior.

text: When a value from a DOM API or optional payload may be `null` or an empty string (e.g., `getAttribute()` returns `string | null`, a destructured event field is optional) and must be assigned to a `string | undefined` property, a DOM string property like `textContent`, or parsed, do not use a type assertion to silence TypeScript. Normalize values deliberately: convert `null` to `undefined` (or conditionally omit the property) so runtime APIs never receive `null`; when capturing an element's `textContent` for later restoration, normalize to `''` with `|| ''`. For `getAttribute()` results, decide explicitly how empty strings are treated: use `?? undefined` rather than `|| undefined` when an empty-string value must be preserved (since `getAttribute` distinguishes absent `null` from empty `''`), and use a truthy guard (e.g., `attr ? parseInt(attr, 10) : null`) rather than a `null`-only check when an empty-string attribute should be treated as absent for parsing. Reserve `as string` assertions for cases where a prior guard or default has already established the value is non-null.
reason: TypeScript's optional string property does not accept `null`, and a cast hides the mismatch while still passing an invalid runtime value; DOM string properties like `textContent` also expect a string. Coalescing or conditional inclusion keeps the runtime shape valid, while an assertion is only safe once guard/default logic proves non-nullness. `getAttribute` can return an empty string for empty attributes, so `|| undefined` silently conflates `''` with absent, and a `null`-only check still calls `parseInt('')`, producing `NaN`; empty-string semantics must be deliberate.
common_pattern: Correctly handling the nullable/empty-string edge cases of DOM attribute APIs (`getAttribute()` returning `string | null`) and optional event payloads when consuming them into typed code — avoiding blind type assertions, normalizing `null` to `undefined`, and being explicit about empty-string semantics.

text: Prefer isinstance() for runtime type checks and validation: use isinstance(value, str) (or the most general applicable base type) instead of truthiness checks (`if value:` / `not value`), `type(obj) == Type` identity comparisons, or duck-typing via method presence/catching AttributeError. When checking several possible types, pass a tuple to isinstance() rather than chaining `isinstance(...) or isinstance(...)`. Do not hardcode concrete subclasses in an isinstance check to select behavior/features; instead define an overridable class-level attribute (e.g. a boolean flag defaulting to False) on the base class and let subclasses opt in.
reason: Truthiness shortcuts conflate type validation with non-emptiness and can accept wrong truthy types or reject valid empty strings. isinstance() is idiomatic, faster, subclass-aware, and avoids brittle type identity/duck typing. A fixed isinstance list for behavior selection misses third-party/user-created subclasses, while an extensible base-class attribute lets downstream subclasses participate without modifying core code.
common_pattern: All generalizations concern Python class/type membership checks: how to test whether an object belongs to a type (or family of types) in a robust, idiomatic, and extensible way. The cluster has three distinct sub-patterns: (1) prefer isinstance() over type()/duck-typing checks, (2) avoid hardcoded isinstance class lists for feature selection in favor of extensible base-class opt-in, and (3) avoid duplicating class-matching logic.

text: Define object-shaped type contracts as `interface` rather than `type` aliases, reserving `type` for unions, intersections, mapped types, or other constructs an interface cannot express.
reason: Interfaces are the conventional form for object contracts and provide clearer extension/merging semantics; `type` is better reserved for shapes interfaces cannot express.
common_pattern: TypeScript type/interface declaration conventions: naming, contract form, and generic-type precision.

text: Use lowercase `object` for generic non-primitive object declarations rather than `Object` or `any`.
reason: Lowercase `object` is the TypeScript type for non-primitive values and is more precise than `any` or `Object`.
common_pattern: TypeScript type/interface declaration conventions: naming, contract form, and generic-type precision.

text: Return type annotations must match the actual return shape: use `list`/`List[Model]` for ordered variable-length homogeneous collections, use the concrete type for single-value returns rather than `Tuple[...]`, and update annotations when changing container types (e.g., from `Tuple` to a custom list subclass).
reason: Tuples imply fixed-length heterogeneous records, so using them for variable-length returns or wrapped single values misleads callers and type checkers. Annotations should reflect the real container/return type.
common_pattern: Return type annotations must accurately describe the actual returned value/container shape, especially avoiding misleading `Tuple[...]` annotations for variable-length collections or single-value returns.

text: Functions and methods whose contract implies a boolean (predicates, `isX` helpers) must return a strict boolean: write explicit boolean expressions (`value is not None and value.predicate()`) and, for shared boolean utilities, coerce operands (e.g. `!!x && !!y`) rather than returning a raw falsy operand.
reason: Runtime consumers (and non-TypeScript callers) may receive `None`, `0`, or an object instead of `false`; TypeScript/Python annotations are not enforced at runtime, so the returned value must actually be boolean.
common_pattern: Handling of booleans and presence checks: choosing the check form that matches the value's semantic type (boolean vs. null/absence), guaranteeing boolean-typed return values and flags, and avoiding redundant or misleading coercions (`!!`, `is True`, `1`/`0`).

text: In TypeScript, omit explicit `: void` return type annotations on class methods (especially Stimulus lifecycle methods under `client/src/controllers/`) when TypeScript can infer the void return type; however, explicitly annotate standalone functions with `: void` when they do not return a value to make the contract clear.
reason: Redundant `: void` annotations add noise on simple methods where inference is obvious, while standalone functions benefit from an explicit `: void` contract.
scope: global:TypeScript; project: client/src/controllers Stimulus controllers for lifecycle methods
common_pattern: TypeScript void return handling: how to annotate `: void`, when to rely on inference, and how to handle return statements when no meaningful value is produced.

text: In TypeScript, annotate function parameters and interface method signatures with explicit types rather than relying on implicit `any`. Use `?` to mark optional parameters, and use inline object types (e.g. `options: { pattern: string }`) for simple option objects.
reason: Implicit `any` defeats TypeScript's compile-time checking, weakens IDE autocomplete/signature help, and allows callers to pass incorrect argument types without any error. Explicit annotations document the expected shape and enforce it.
common_pattern: This cluster spans two related but distinct sub-patterns about TypeScript type information: (A) TypeScript signatures must carry explicit type annotations and never rely on implicit `any`, and (B) JSDoc in TypeScript/TS-bound code should describe meaning rather than duplicate type information that TypeScript already enforces.

text: When overriding a method defined in a base class or mixin, keep return type annotations consistent with the base definition—either annotate both the base method and its override or leave both unannotated.
reason: Inconsistent annotations between a base method and its override can confuse readers and type checkers, and imply an API contract that does not exist in the base class.
common_pattern: Rules about how to document and keep consistency with base-class/framework methods when overriding them: documentation should not restate inherited behavior, but should capture override-specific intent, caveats, provenance, required parent calls, and annotation consistency.

text: In Stimulus controllers, model structured data as `Object`-typed values with a matching object default (e.g., `{ type: Object, default: {} }`) rather than declaring a `String` value and encoding/decoding JSON manually. Rely on Stimulus's built-in value parsing instead of manual `JSON.parse` plus fallback or shape-validation code, and document the value as the typed object rather than as a 'JSON string containing X'.
reason: An Object-typed value gives consumers a correctly typed object directly, avoids duplicated/serialized-string boilerplate, keeps the declared type faithful to the actual data shape, and eliminates manual parsing and fallback logic that is error-prone and hard to keep consistent.
common_pattern: In Stimulus controllers, structured data should be modeled as Object-typed values so the framework parses it, instead of encoding it as a JSON string and hand-rolling JSON.parse/serialization and fallback or shape-validation logic.

text: Source TypeScript types from the standard, canonical providers: reference built-in lib types (enabling the required lib in tsconfig) for platform/Intl APIs instead of declaring duplicate local interfaces, add the corresponding @types/* package to devDependencies for JavaScript dependencies that lack bundled types, and import third-party libraries/types via explicit ES module imports rather than relying on ambient globals or commented-out imports. Do not add @types/* packages whose types are not actually used.
reason: Using canonical type sources (built-in libs, @types packages, explicit imports) keeps type checking accurate, makes dependencies visible, and avoids maintaining stale duplicate declarations or bloating the dependency tree with unused type packages.
common_pattern: Sourcing TypeScript types from canonical, standard places rather than ad-hoc workarounds: use built-in lib types for platform APIs, add @types/* devDependencies for JS packages, import libraries explicitly instead of relying on globals, and configure tsconfig lib correctly when overriding it.

text: For non-standard browser globals, augment the global interface (`Window`, `JQuery`) in the project's shared TypeScript declaration file instead of casting to `any` at call sites. If the global is untyped, declare it as `any` with a comment noting that proper types should be added later.
reason: Centralizes global typings, preserves TypeScript type checking, and avoids scattered unsafe `any` casts.
common_pattern: Handling non-standard browser globals in TypeScript by augmenting global interfaces (Window, JQuery) in a shared declaration file instead of using `any` casts, with complementary guidance for untyped globals and optional globals.

text: Bind optional globals to a local `const` before use so that TypeScript's type narrowing from the guard applies to subsequent usages.
reason: Narrowing a mutable property like `window.telepath` does not persist across statements, so a local variable is required for the null-check to be effective for later calls.
common_pattern: Handling non-standard browser globals in TypeScript by augmenting global interfaces (Window, JQuery) in a shared declaration file instead of using `any` casts, with complementary guidance for untyped globals and optional globals.

text: React components must declare explicit, precise TypeScript types for their props, state, and children: define a props interface/type, type `children` as `React.ReactNode` (not `any[]`), avoid `any`/implicit `any` in prop interfaces, provide explicit initial values for typed `useState` (never rely on uninitialized generics), declare optional-prop defaults via `defaultProps` (not inline destructuring fallbacks), and remove stale `as any` casts once dependency type definitions cover the required props.
reason: Explicit, precise types catch misuse at call sites, enable IDE tooling, and maintain type safety across the component tree; `any` and uninitialized/undefined-typed state defeat compile-time checking and mask invalid usages; stale casts and inline defaults become out of sync with actual runtime contracts.
common_pattern: React components should expose explicit, precise type and prop contracts — fully typed props/state/children without `any` or implicit typing, stale casts removed, defaults declared, and runtime prop validation preserved for non-TypeScript consumers.

text: Handle UUIDs as native UUID values: store model UUID fields with Django `UUIDField` rather than string/character fields; keep generated or mapped UUIDs as `uuid.UUID` objects rather than converting to `str` unless a string representation is explicitly required; and generate random UUIDs for values that must be unique without a database lookup instead of deriving them from session or user-scoped identifiers.
reason: `UUIDField` is the idiomatic Django storage type for UUID values, native `uuid.UUID` avoids unnecessary type conversions and preserves correct ORM/database handling, and randomly generated UUIDs guarantee uniqueness without a DB query while avoiding collisions from user-scoped derivations.
common_pattern: Idiomatic UUID handling: use native UUID types for storage and in-memory values, and generate random UUIDs for database-independent uniqueness instead of string or session-derived alternatives.

text: Represent fixed sets of HTTP methods as `http.HTTPMethod` enum members rather than raw strings or runtime-normalized string properties. Store/compare canonical values, never derive an uppercased copy on each request.
reason: Enum members are canonical in-memory values, so they avoid per-request string allocation from normalization properties, provide stronger typing (typos raise AttributeError instead of silently comparing against an invalid string), and align with modern typed Python. Historical use of raw strings in Django predates `http.HTTPMethod` (Python 3.10) and easy enum usage; matching that legacy convention is not required in new code.
common_pattern: How to represent HTTP methods (and similar fixed value sets) in Django-facing code: avoid per-request string normalization, and choose a canonical representation. The cluster shows an evolution from 'store uppercase strings' to the resolved outcome 'use http.HTTPMethod enum members', with all participants agreeing that per-request normalization/derivation of uppercased copies is wrong.

text: For optional numeric index state (e.g., highlighted/previewed index), represent 'no selection' with the component's established numeric sentinel such as `-1`, keep the value typed as `number`, and test selection with `index >= 0` instead of `undefined` or `typeof value !== 'undefined'`. Reset values should use the same sentinel used for initialization and comparisons.
reason: Avoids `number`/`undefined` type mismatches, keeps index-based state and comparisons consistent, and makes the no-selection value explicit.
common_pattern: Use a numeric sentinel (-1) for 'no selection' in optional numeric index state, keep the state typed as number, and test selection with `index >= 0` rather than `undefined` or `typeof` checks.

text: When a parameter's default value is `None`, annotate it explicitly as optional (`T | None`) rather than a bare `T`; use the PEP 604 `X | Y` union syntax instead of `typing.Optional[X]` / `typing.Union[X, Y]`.
reason: A `None` default is not assignable to a bare `T` annotation, so the annotation is type-incorrect. Since Python 3.9 support has been dropped, the concise PEP 604 `|` syntax is available and preferred over the older `Optional[T]`/`Union[T, None]` forms.
common_pattern: Optional/None-valued type annotations must be explicitly marked as optional rather than leaving a bare type annotation that excludes None; the modern PEP 604 `X | None` syntax is the preferred spelling now that Python 3.9 support is dropped.

text: Add type annotations to method parameters and return values. Annotate every concrete implementation and subclass, not just the base class (e.g. `expand_db_attributes`, `expand_db_attributes_many`, `get_many`; `Component.render_html(self, parent_context: Mapping[str, Any] = None) -> str`), importing types like `Mapping`/`Any` from `typing` as needed.
reason: Consistent annotations across all implementations enable static type checking, IDE support, and refactor safety, and make the component API self-documenting; annotating only the base class leaves the benefits partially unrealized.
common_pattern: Adding explicit type annotations to method signatures so the API is self-documenting and statically checkable, including every concrete implementation/subclass rather than only the base class, and using structured types (TypedDict) for dict parameters with known keys.

text: When a parameter is a dict with known keys (e.g. parsed HTML attributes), define and use a `TypedDict` to document its structure instead of leaving it as a plain dict.
reason: Untyped dict parameters force readers to reverse-engineer expected keys and value types and hide errors from static analysis; a `TypedDict` makes the structure explicit and checkable.
common_pattern: Adding explicit type annotations to method signatures so the API is self-documenting and statically checkable, including every concrete implementation/subclass rather than only the base class, and using structured types (TypedDict) for dict parameters with known keys.

text: When normalizing/coercing values that may be either scalars or containers, accept any non-string iterable (e.g. type against `collections.abc.Iterable` rather than a concrete `list`) so sibling block implementations stay consistent, but explicitly exclude `str`/`bytes` (or use an explicit container check such as `isinstance(v, (list, tuple))`). Never rely on a bare iterability check like `hasattr(v, '__iter__')` to decide whether to join/iterate, because strings are iterable and would be split into individual characters.
reason: Merges the complementary halves of the cluster: being permissive about which iterable types are accepted (avoiding over-restriction to `list`) while still guarding against strings, which are iterable but semantically scalar. Ignoring the string guard corrupts values (e.g. `'Hello world'` becomes `'H,e,l,l,o,...'`) and breaks downstream CSV export.
common_pattern: Type-checking/coercion policy for values that may be either scalars or containers: prefer broad iterable acceptance, but explicitly exclude `str`/`bytes` so strings are treated as scalars rather than container-like sequences.

text: Navigation callbacks declared on a component's props interface (e.g., `navigate`) must be typed to return `Promise<void>` to accurately reflect their asynchronous implementation.
reason: Keeps prop typings accurate, allows callers to await navigation, and ensures type safety/consistency across the interface.
common_pattern: Navigation/navigation-callback props on component interfaces should be typed as async (returning `Promise<void>`) to match their implementation contract.

text: Mark a prop as required (`.isRequired`) in PropTypes whenever the component cannot function meaningfully without it — including nested fields inside `PropTypes.shape` — and use optional types only for genuinely optional values.
reason: Declaring truly-required props (and required shape fields) as `.isRequired` documents the component's real contract and surfaces caller misuse early, rather than silently producing partial or broken renders.
common_pattern: Both generalizations express the same principle: PropTypes should mark as `.isRequired` any prop or shape field that the component meaningfully depends on, using optional types only for genuinely optional values.

text: Type parameters or variables used as DOM element identifiers/selectors as `string`, even when the identifier value is numeric, because DOM lookup APIs and selectors expect string identifiers.
reason: DOM lookup APIs and CSS selectors operate on strings; using `number` is semantically incorrect and can cause type or refactor issues.
common_pattern: Naming and typing of DOM element references: variables holding DOM nodes/queries should be named by their semantic role or actual element type (never by an assumed HTML tag suffix), and identifiers used for DOM lookups should be typed as strings regardless of numeric content.

text: In tests, exercise the real production implementation rather than duplicating it or creating test-only scaffolding. Import and use existing production classes (which already expose the needed internal state) and plain built-in values where they suffice; do not copy or redefine the implementation inside the test file, and avoid defining test-only subclasses or helper classes unless required by the behavior under test. If the implementation is not importable, refactor production code to expose it or test it through a public API; do not import future or nonexistent APIs.
reason: Testing duplicated or substitute implementations does not verify the actual production code, leading to false confidence; using real classes avoids diverging test scaffolding and keeps tests focused and coupled to the behavior under test.
common_pattern: Test-only scaffolding/minimization: avoid inventing custom classes or runtime guards in tests when existing production classes, plain built-in values, or the class hierarchy can express the behavior under test directly.

text: Add focused tests for the validation/error/exception branches that are actually reachable in new or changed code, asserting the exact failure behavior (e.g., the precise exception type and message) alongside the happy-path test. Cover cases such as a guard raising on an invalid input state, a `clean_*` form method rejecting bad input, an invalid query-parameter combination, a nonexistent/invalid identifier, or a lookup helper that raises because a required default/configuration object is absent (set up that absence explicitly rather than relying on behavior copied from another module). Conversely, remove tests that assert failure/validation cases that are impossible by construction (e.g., validation errors for automatically generated unique values). Testing only reachable error branches keeps coverage meaningful and the error contract locked down, while tests for unreachable failure paths add maintenance burden and become misleading when guarantees change.
reason: Reachable error branches encode important behavior and can regress unnoticed without targeted tests, so they should be exercised and asserted directly. Tests for failure paths that cannot occur by construction add maintenance burden and mislead when the underlying guarantees change.
common_pattern: All four generalizations address testing of validation/error branches: three require adding focused tests that trigger validation guards and assert the error contract, while the fourth requires removing tests that assert failure paths impossible by construction. Together they form one principle about which error branches deserve test coverage — those reachable given the code's guarantees.

text: When testing copy operations, create populated source instances and re-fetch the copied object from the database, then assert persisted copy semantics: excluded/ignored fields or relations are actually omitted or correct—not merely that the copy operation does not raise. For Wagtail page copy actions specifically, verify that revision-managed fields such as `draft_title` reflect the new values and that `GenericRelation` related objects are not copied or associated with the new page.
reason: A no-crash test does not exercise exclusion/ignore behavior. Regression assertions that re-fetch the copied object and inspect its persisted state guard against broad `save()` overwrites and ensure relations that should not be duplicated are correctly ignored.
scope: copy-operation tests (Wagtail page copy actions and general copy-exclusion tests)
common_pattern: Both generalizations require behavior-verification tests to assert the post-operation state of the copied object, rather than merely checking that the operation does not raise. They converge on the same testing principle: prove exclusion/ignore behavior by inspecting the resulting object.

text: When adding a new option, configuration parameter, optional parameter, fallback/behavioral change, or configurable limit/setting that can be disabled (e.g. None), to an existing public API, method, or widget, add automated tests that exercise the new behavior beyond the default case: include non-default values, omitted/fallback cases, the disabled value (asserting whether the check is skipped or still enforced), and relevant boundary cases such as specifying the parameter more than once.
reason: Existing tests typically use defaults and therefore cannot catch regressions or unexpected behavior in newly introduced API surface, especially edge cases like omitted, duplicate, disabled, or non-default values. The disabled-value test pins down intended short-circuit or enforcement behavior.
common_pattern: New public API surface—whether a widget option, configuration flag, method parameter, or behavioral fallback—must be covered by automated tests that exercise the new behavior beyond the default/happy path.

text: When a utility or form behavior accepts multiple input shapes (e.g. flat choices vs. grouped dict choices) or has cardinality-dependent paths (e.g. exactly one permitted collection vs. multiple), add tests for every supported variant rather than a single general test. Reuse existing Wagtail models that already configure choices fields (e.g. EventPage, FullFeaturedSnippet) before defining a new test model.
reason: Format- and cardinality-dependent behavior is easy to get wrong, and single-path tests hide regressions in the untested branches.
common_pattern: Testing conventions for code that handles multiple input shapes or choice sets: exhaustive coverage of every supported variant, plus direct assertions on the complete expected output.

text: Run and smoke-test affected code in a local development environment before committing or submitting changes. Verify that newly referenced symbols are actually imported and that the module runs; for rendered or interactive changes, also verify them locally rather than relying solely on static diff review, since rendering issues, event-handler typos, invalid event types, and similar runtime problems only surface when the code is actually run.
reason: Running the affected code locally catches missing imports, execution errors, silent rendering issues, and interactive-event mistakes before review, preventing broken or non-functional changes from being merged.
common_pattern: Testing discipline for Wagtail view/template changes: changes to view rendering or templates must be accompanied by automated tests that exercise the view through the test client and assert both the rendered HTML output and the context supplied to the template (with new behavior tests failing against the pre-change implementation), while test templates themselves are kept minimal and free of debug or test-only markup.

text: Tests for admin view/form actions — including Wagtail admin inline panel/formset regression tests — should drive requests through the actual admin view/form flow by submitting a real POST to the admin edit view and asserting the intended state change or formset behavior (e.g., object actually removed). Include a success-path case, not only blocked/failure cases; do not invoke model methods directly or validate a plain Django ModelForm. Also avoid fields='__all__' on a model with no own fields, since the resulting empty form cannot become invalid and therefore cannot exercise the fix.
reason: Plain ModelForms and direct model calls bypass the admin view/formset processing that can mutate state or trigger the regression, and empty forms cannot exercise invalid-state behavior. Success-path assertions are needed because the success path is the primary behavior being tested.
scope: admin view/form test design, including Wagtail admin inline panel/formset regression tests
common_pattern: Both generalizations concern how to design tests for admin view actions: exercise the actual view/form flow and cover the success path (rather than bypassing the view with direct model calls or only testing failure cases).

text: Add explicit tests for the absence of optional data/inputs, including the default/fallback path, when that absence changes behavior or rendering: assert that the expected empty/default structure (of the same type) is returned, that methods returning no-custom-configuration results still return a valid value rather than breaking, and that standalone utilities parsing request headers or user-agent values behave correctly when no relevant header is present (test the utility directly, not only via its callers). If the optional input path is not needed, remove it instead of leaving it untested.
reason: Untested optional branches and default/fallback paths increase maintenance cost and regression risk; explicit absence cases document the intended behavior and protect rendering/behavior branches, and utilities extracted from original call sites need their own basic test suite.
common_pattern: Test optional/absent data branches explicitly; do not leave supported optional inputs or optional fields untested, and remove unused optional functionality rather than keeping it uncovered.

text: When code accesses a nullable foreign key, include a test case where that foreign key is null and assert the code handles the missing relationship gracefully (for example, no error, response 200, and empty rendered cell where applicable).
reason: Nullable foreign keys are a common edge case that can cause runtime errors such as AttributeError or KeyError, and explicit null-case tests prevent regressions in view logic and related-field rendering.
common_pattern: Tests for code paths that access nullable foreign keys should explicitly cover the null case to verify graceful handling and prevent runtime or rendering regressions.

text: When testing expected exceptions or deprecation warnings with context-manager assertions, perform setup (e.g., object construction) before entering the context and scope the context to only the operation expected to raise or emit the signal. For expected exceptions, place post-call assertions after the `with` block, since statements following the raising call inside the block never execute; assert the specific exception type expected, and use `assertRaisesMessage` with the expected message for exceptions the project itself raises; avoid bare `assertRaises` with the broad `Exception` class. For deprecation warnings, use `self.assertWarnsMessage(WarningClass, expected_message)` instead of manually capturing warnings with `warnings.catch_warnings(record=True)`, and scope the assertion to only the operation that emits the warning (e.g., `render()`), excluding setup such as object instantiation.
reason: Wrapping setup inside the assertion context can make tests pass for the wrong reason, and assertions placed after a raising statement inside the block are dead code that silently weakens coverage. Specific exception/warning classes and messages keep tests from masking unrelated errors and make the message part of the tested contract. For warnings, `assertWarnsMessage` is more idiomatic and concise than manual `catch_warnings` capture, and scoping it to the emitting operation proves the warning comes from the intended code path.
scope: test code (expected exceptions and deprecation warnings)
common_pattern: Proper use of Python assertions and assertion-based testing: reserving `assert` for internal invariants (never runtime/user-input validation), and structuring tests so that exceptions, their types, and their messages are verified precisely rather than loosely or redundantly.

text: Add tests for new and existing helper/utility functions that cover the full range of supported inputs, intentional edge cases (e.g., URL components deliberately dropped or preserved, non-model values, basic typo-catching cases), and graceful handling of unsupported or missing inputs; reuse existing related test modules rather than creating new test scaffolding.
reason: Comprehensive helper/utility tests document intended behavior, catch typos and regressions, lock in the expected contract for edge cases, and keep tests discoverable while reducing setup cost.
common_pattern: New utility functions must be accompanied by unit tests that cover edge cases, all supported input formats, and graceful handling of unsupported or missing inputs.

text: For any conditionally rendered UI—whether gated by a feature flag/setting, translation availability (e.g., locale selector for translatable models), or user permissions—explicitly assert both states: the enabled/present case (control/UI is rendered) and the disabled/absent case (it is not). Verify the user-visible rendered output rather than only backing form/object state. This is especially important when per-model view logic is consolidated into shared/generic base views (locale UI can be silently dropped) and after permission context/template refactors (permission-gated controls must still render for permitted users). Positive and negative assertions may live in separate test methods per existing test organization; a negative-only test can pass due to a selector typo or unrelated removal and misses regressions where a disabled control is still rendered.
reason: Conditional UI presence and absence are both conditional on feature flags, model translatability, or permissions; testing only one branch leaves the other unprotected against regression. Negative-only tests can pass spuriously, while positive coverage ensures the enabled path actually works.
scope: Conditional UI tests (feature flags/settings, translation/locale, permission-gated admin UI, bulk actions, shared view refactors)
common_pattern: Permission-gated UI controls must be explicitly verified across both denied and allowed/changed permission states, rather than only checking warning text or assuming rendering still works.

text: In tests, assert explicit hard-coded literal expected values using exact assertions (e.g. assertEqual). Do not derive expected values from production constants, the code under test, or helper logic, and reserve substring/membership assertions (assertIn) for cases where multiple acceptable values may legitimately appear. In form field choice tests (e.g. Wagtail form/settings tests), assert the complete expected list of `(value, label)` tuples with explicit literal values rather than splitting assertions across extracted value sets and label mappings or re-deriving values programmatically.
reason: Literal expectations avoid tautological tests that pass even when production logic is wrong, while exact assertions and full expected-list comparisons catch unexpected extra output, ordering changes, formatting regressions, and label regressions that substring or value-only checks miss.
scope: global (with specific guidance for Wagtail form/settings tests)
common_pattern: Tests should specify expected behavior as explicit, literal values and use exact assertions for deterministic output, rather than deriving expectations from production code/constants or relying on loose substring checks.

text: When a Wagtail feature supports a customizable hook with a default fallback—such as form-class hooks via `getattr(model, "<hook>_form_class", DefaultForm)` or avatar/Gravatar URL helpers (`get_gravatar_url` defaulting `default_params` to `{"d": "mp"}` and the custom `get_avatar_url` hook)—preserve the default fallback behavior and add tests covering both the custom override path and the default fallback path, including the Gravatar/static fallback.
reason: Hook overrides and fallback logic change runtime behavior based on model configuration or settings; without tests, regressions in either the custom hook path or the default fallback path can go unnoticed.
scope: Wagtail customizable hooks with default fallbacks, including form-class customization hooks and avatar/Gravatar URL helpers (`wagtail/users/utils.py`, `wagtail/admin/templatetags/wagtailadmin_tags.py`)
common_pattern: Avatar/Gravatar URL generation must preserve and verify its default fallback behavior across custom hook and non-hook paths.

text: When changing a view or template's rendering behavior — including context flags, view modes, profile-derived values (e.g., keyboard-shortcuts-enabled state passed to the keyboard shortcuts dialog), or view-provided context variables — add or update tests that exercise the view through the test client and assert both: (1) the exact context passed to the template (whether computed or request-controlled, covering default behavior and explicitly supplied request values where applicable, e.g., in `test_keyboard_shortcuts.py`), and (2) the resulting rendered HTML/markup. Verify the context wiring from the user profile, not just that the template renders. New-behavior tests should fail against the pre-change implementation.
reason: Context wiring alone does not prove the template adapts its output, and rendering alone does not prove the view supplies the correct values — especially profile-derived flags such as keyboard-shortcuts-enabled state. Asserting both the exact context values (including defaults and request-controlled overrides) and the rendered markup, with a test that fails against the previous behavior, catches regressions in view/template integration such as ignored profile settings, unapplied modes, silent mis-defaulting, or incorrect computed values.
common_pattern: Testing discipline for Wagtail view/template changes: changes to view rendering or templates must be accompanied by automated tests that exercise the view through the test client and assert both the rendered HTML output and the context supplied to the template (with new behavior tests failing against the pre-change implementation), while test templates themselves are kept minimal and free of debug or test-only markup.

text: Tests that register document-level event listeners, keyboard shortcut managers, custom event collections, signal handlers, or other global hooks/callbacks/receivers must clean up that global state in a guaranteed mechanism (e.g., `afterEach` or a `finally` block) so cleanup occurs even when the test fails. For event listeners, register and reset collected events in `beforeEach`, and reset global listeners/shortcut managers in `afterEach` to prevent cross-test state leakage.
reason: Global event listeners and other global state can persist between tests, causing false positives/negatives, order-dependent failures, and coupling assertions to event timing or controller internals. Explicit lifecycle setup/teardown with guaranteed cleanup preserves test isolation and makes event assertions reliable even when tests fail.
scope: JavaScript tests for controllers/components that dispatch custom events or bind global/document-level listeners, and any test suite that modifies global state such as signal handlers, hooks, callbacks, or receivers
common_pattern: Tests must reverse any global state changes they introduce by unregistering or disconnecting registered resources in a guaranteed cleanup block such as `finally`, so cleanup runs even when assertions fail and does not leak into other tests.

text: In `client/src/includes/*.test.js`, add test coverage for every `data-*` attribute that alters component behavior (e.g. DOM hooks like `data-breadcrumb-item`, or selector attributes like `data-header-selector`). Construct fixture HTML with the attribute on the component root (and a target id on an outer ancestor for selector attributes), initialize the component, and assert the resulting behavior — such as the element being handled or the listener being attached to the intended target. In breadcrumb component tests specifically, assert that `data-header-selector` accepts any CSS selector and that the resolved ancestor element receives the interactive event listeners.
reason: Fixture markup that merely contains the attribute does not verify the implementation consumes it; testing configurable attributes — including arbitrary selector values — prevents regressions in attribute-based initialization, selection, and event wiring. This merges the breadcrumb-specific selector assertion into the broader data-attribute test rule.
common_pattern: All three generalizations concern the same PR and the same principle: in the client includes test files, data-* attributes that drive component behavior (DOM hooks, selector configuration) must be explicitly covered by tests with constructed fixture markup that exercises the attribute-driven behavior.

text: When testing a `data-*` attribute selector used with `element.closest()`, choose an outer target element type that cannot match a generic tag selector (e.g., use `div` instead of `header`) so the test actually exercises the configured selector attribute and not incidental tag-name matching.
reason: Avoids a false pass caused by tag-name matching rather than the configured selector; this remains distinct from general data-attribute coverage because it addresses a specific selector/closest test construction pitfall.
common_pattern: Resolving a consumer-supplied CSS selector from a data attribute via `Element.closest()` — covering both the implementation pattern and how to test it without a tag-name false pass.

text: Omit the controller, module, or function name from nested `describe` and `it` descriptions; rely on the parent describe block and the test file context to supply the identifier.
reason: Jest appends parent describe names in console output and snapshots, so repeating the name adds noise and maintenance work.
common_pattern: Jest/mocha test organization conventions: use `describe` blocks (keyed to the unit, method, or behavior under test) to structure tests, keep nesting shallow, place new tests inside existing matching describe blocks rather than creating new ones, and avoid redundant naming/decoration inside those blocks.

text: In tests, explicitly clear or reset cached state that can leak between tests—Django/framework caches, class-level caches, and `@cached_property` values—in `setUp`/`tearDown` or immediately before re-accessing the value. Clear `@cached_property` with `del` (guarded by `try`/`except AttributeError` when order-dependent) and reset class-level caches through known reset hooks or dedicated test helpers/public APIs rather than mutating private internals.
reason: Cached values can retain state from other tests or prior locale/settings, causing order-dependent failures; explicit cache clearing keeps tests isolated and deterministic.
common_pattern: Testing cache-related behavior requires explicit cache-state control for test isolation, plus assertions through production code paths (typically query counts and downstream effects) that prove caching and invalidation actually work.

text: When testing caching or cache invalidation, exercise the production request/view path and assert the observable caching effect: use query-count assertions such as `assertNumQueries` to verify cold-cache misses and warm-cache hits (repeated operation performs zero queries), and for invalidation assert downstream values that depend on the cleared cache rather than only that the cache was cleared. Do not simulate cache hits by assigning cache attributes directly.
reason: Query-count and downstream-value assertions verify the actual caching mechanism and catch regressions where cached lookups still query the database or invalidation leaves dependent values stale.
common_pattern: Testing cache-related behavior requires explicit cache-state control for test isolation, plus assertions through production code paths (typically query counts and downstream effects) that prove caching and invalidation actually work.

text: Test docstrings and comments must accurately describe the specific scenario and asserted outcome of that test — including error status codes, settings/flags involved, and unchanged state — and must never be copy-pasted from a sibling test or contradict the assertion. Rename or rewrite the docstring whenever the tested behaviour changes.
reason: Names and docstrings that contradict the assertions (or describe a different test's steps) mislead maintainers about the real contract, hide bugs in the test itself, and make failures hard to interpret.
common_pattern: Test documentation (docstrings and comments) must accurately and specifically describe what each test actually verifies, and should be expressed as docstrings rather than inline comments when the test name alone is insufficient.

text: In tests, toggle settings/feature flags with Django's `override_settings` at the appropriate scope—class-level when shared by multiple tests, method-level for one-off variations—and avoid patching internal helper functions or mutating shared test settings. Cover both the default/enabled path and the overridden/disabled path when the setting changes behavior.
reason: This exercises the real setting-lookup path, keeps default behavior covered for the rest of the suite, reduces duplication, and prevents silent regressions in disabled/overridden configurations.
common_pattern: Conventions for handling Django/Wagtail settings and feature flags: override them at the correct scope in tests, cover both default and non-default behavior, and manage documentation/lifecycle when settings become user-facing or stable.

text: When overriding attributes of a helper-created object (e.g., a request from `get_dummy_request()`), mutate the existing container in place (e.g., `request.META.update({...})`) instead of reassigning it wholesale.
reason: Reassigning the whole attribute discards the realistic baseline the helper was introduced to supply, defeating its purpose; `.update()` preserves existing keys while applying test-specific overrides.
common_pattern: Wagtail test-suite conventions for constructing and configuring request objects: prefer project-standard helpers over ad-hoc construction, and preserve helper-provided baselines when overriding values.

text: Ensure test coverage is scoped to the module's responsibility: new utility modules (e.g., a registry, factory, or state container) must ship with a corresponding unit test file covering their public functions. Compatibility/import-shim packages should only be tested for the shims themselves, not for downstream application behavior.
reason: Untested utility modules are easy to break in refactors, while shim packages should not own tests beyond their shim responsibility, keeping test coverage aligned with module purpose.
common_pattern: Guidelines for test code organization and integrity: keep test-only helpers separate from production code, test the real production implementation rather than duplicates, and scope test coverage appropriately to module responsibility.

text: In tests, assert exact occurrence counts when verifying rendered elements or templates: pass an explicit `count` (usually `count=1`) to assertion helpers like `assertContains` and `assertTemplateUsed`, keep those counts unchanged during unrelated edits, and ensure the test fixture HTML nests counted elements inside the selector's matching container so the count reflects the real DOM structure.
reason: Prevents weak presence-only assertions and accidental count changes from masking regressions or duplicate rendering, while making the test's structural expectations explicit.
common_pattern: Tests that assert rendered output should use explicit, intentional occurrence counts (typically `count=1`) in assertion helpers, and the fixture/DOM structure must support those counts so they reflect real behavior.

text: For Stimulus controllers that compute or filter based on a value, explicitly handle the empty/zero/cleared input state: clear any stale target content (including server-rendered values) instead of leaving it, remove the corresponding URL query param when applicable, and add tests that cover clearing a previously entered value and verifying the target results update.
reason: Empty/cleared value handling is a distinct state transition that must be implemented intentionally and tested explicitly; otherwise stale server-rendered or client-computed content and orphaned query params can persist and regress unnoticed.
scope: Stimulus controllers, with tests in client/src/controllers tests
common_pattern: Stimulus controllers must explicitly handle empty/zero/cleared-value states, both in runtime behavior and in test coverage, rather than leaving stale content or untested clearing transitions.

text: When testing string parsing or normalization functions, include edge cases such as multi-word unquoted input and malformed delimiters (e.g., unclosed quotes) in addition to valid quoted inputs.
reason: Multi-word unquoted inputs and malformed delimiters may be parsed differently from valid quoted inputs; testing them ensures correct normalization and prevents parser regressions or crashes.
common_pattern: Tests for string parsing/normalization should be thorough: cover edge-case inputs and ensure test data is correctly structured to avoid false coverage.

text: In test fixtures using lists of string literals (e.g., in Python), ensure each element is separated by a comma; missing commas cause implicit string concatenation, silently merging elements and reducing test coverage.
reason: Missing commas between string literals in a list cause Python's implicit string concatenation to merge them into one element, so the test exercises different data than intended.
common_pattern: Tests for string parsing/normalization should be thorough: cover edge-case inputs and ensure test data is correctly structured to avoid false coverage.

text: Structure tests around a single behavior: split test methods that cover multiple distinct scenarios, cases, or configuration states into one test per scenario, and place assertions in the test class dedicated to the behavior/configuration under test (e.g., default/enabled behavior asserted in the enable-behavior test class, not in the disable test).
reason: Separate, behavior-named tests isolate failures, make intent clear from the test name, and prevent an early assertion or unrelated state from masking other cases.
common_pattern: Test organization should be driven by 'one behavior per test': distinct behaviors/scenarios/configurations get their own focused test, while variations of the SAME behavior that share setup/assertions are consolidated (via parameterization/table-driven cases) rather than duplicated. Both halves aim to make failures localize to an intended behavior and keep test intent scannable.

text: Test widget behavior through the real form/field integration: instantiate the final form (e.g. a `WagtailAdminModelForm` subclass) or the constructed field and assert on the resulting widget (`form.fields[field].widget`, `block.field.widget`), test defaults by omitting the widget override so the default-resolution path runs, and avoid relying on `field_options` internals, `hasattr` checks, or manually assigned attributes on bare widget instances.
reason: Internal option state and hand-stubbed widget instances only prove isolated behavior and miss regressions in how widgets resolve configuration (e.g. ForeignKey `to_field`, default substitution) through the real form/field wiring.
common_pattern: Django/Wagtail widget and form-field conventions: use the framework's standard extension points for widgets (pass widget *classes*, expose `widget=`, avoid redundant default overrides, prefer built-ins over custom duplicates), and verify widget behavior through real form/field integration rather than bare widget instances or internal option state.

text: When testing Django form widget rendering, assert the rendered HTML contract: verify default rendering with `assertInHTML`, verify caller-supplied `attrs` overrides are preserved, use `@override_settings` with `assertIn`/`assertNotIn` to check settings-dependent `data-*` attributes, and assert boolean attributes as standalone names when true and absent when false rather than expecting `=""` in raw HTML.
reason: Protects the widget's HTML output contract, ensures customization hooks and settings-dependent behavior remain functional, and avoids Django boolean-attribute rendering confusion.
common_pattern: Django/Wagtail widget tests: where to place/group them and how to assert rendered HTML contracts

text: In event-driven tests, only register mocks or event listeners that are actually asserted on. When asserting, verify the specific event target, event type, and detail/payload for each relevant event (including custom and lifecycle events and error paths), rather than relying on call count alone.
reason: Unasserted mocks/listeners add noise and can imply behavior is tested when it is not. Vague assertions miss regressions such as listeners attached to the wrong element, missing or incorrect event detail, or untested custom-event dispatch paths.
scope: test files for DOM/event-driven controllers and components (Jest/JSDOM)
common_pattern: Event-driven tests must be intentional: only create mocks/listeners that will be asserted on, and make assertions specific about event target, type, and detail/payload across all relevant event paths.

text: When writing inline HTML fixtures in tests, especially Stimulus/JS controller tests, keep them minimal and well-formed: include only the DOM elements, attributes, and text needed for the test; omit irrelevant CSS classes and content; keep attributes inside the opening tag and text content between opening and closing tags; use valid closing tags; align opening and closing tags; and indent nested markup with consistent two-space indentation while avoiding excessive nesting or over-indentation. Collapse simple/short elements onto one line, and for larger fixtures put attributes on separate indented lines, except when the test asserts exact HTML output—there keep the opening tag's attributes on a single line to avoid whitespace/newline mismatches.
reason: Keeps tests focused on behavior, reduces noise, improves readability, and prevents malformed fixtures or whitespace-sensitive exact-output assertions from silently failing.
scope: test files containing inline HTML fixtures
common_pattern: Hygiene for inline HTML fixtures in tests: keep fixtures minimal, focused, well-formed, and consistently formatted for readability and reliable test behavior.

text: For file/spreadsheet export tests, parse the exported file (e.g. with `openpyxl.load_workbook`) and assert it contains only the filtered/expected records; do not rely solely on asserting the download URL contains filter parameters.
reason: URL assertions only prove filter parameters reached the link, not that the generated export honored them; parsing the file catches regressions in export generation.
common_pattern: Export functionality must faithfully respect the active filter scope — both in the implementation (distinct URL/query parameters per export scope) and in verification (tests that parse the exported file, not just the download URL).

text: When asserting that rendered HTML contains a URL, build the expected URL with the same helper the template/render path uses: use `django.utils.html.escape` (and `urlencode` for query parameters) for HTML-escaped query-string URLs, and `versioned_static()` for static asset/script URLs.
reason: Rendered HTML escapes query-string separators like `&` to `&` and rewrites static asset paths to versioned URLs; hardcoded, unescaped, or unversioned expected URLs will not match and will be brittle.
scope: Django/Wagtail tests asserting rendered HTML URL or static-asset inclusion
common_pattern: Tests asserting that rendered HTML contains a URL should construct the expected URL using the same encoding/versioning helper used during rendering, so the assertion matches the actual HTML output instead of hardcoded or unescaped values.

text: When changing page explorer reordering/ordering behavior, validate it by adding/updating tests that cover both same-page-type and mixed-page-type parent/child hierarchies, and by manually exercising the real sort-menu-order workflow in the admin UI to confirm the resulting messages and actions.
reason: Page reordering behavior can differ depending on whether parent and child pages share a page type, and the sorting/menu UI depends on runtime JS interactions that unit tests may not fully cover.
scope: project-specific for Wagtail admin page explorer reordering/ordering changes
common_pattern: Validation requirements for changes to Wagtail page reordering/ordering behavior: automated test coverage across page-type hierarchy variants, plus manual exercise of the real admin ordering/menu workflow.
