reason: Hardcoded localhost URLs make integration tests brittle: developers who expose the backend on non-default ports or test remote instances must edit source to run the tests.
common_pattern: Integration tests that navigate to a backend/Wagtail instance must derive the target origin from configuration (an environment variable, e.g. TEST_ORIGIN) instead of hardcoding a localhost URL/port.

text: When PostCSS plugins are added to or changed in the main Webpack config, mirror the same plugin list in the Storybook Webpack/PostCSS configuration.
reason: Keeps the application and Storybook CSS processing consistent, preventing Storybook from rendering components with different styling behavior than the app.
common_pattern: PostCSS plugin configuration must stay synchronized between the main Webpack config and the Storybook Webpack/PostCSS config.

text: Only add type-scale classes (e.g. `.h1`–`.h6`) to the Tailwind type-scale plugin when the heading level is officially defined by the design system; omit unofficial levels until formally added.
reason: Prevents committing the codebase to speculative design tokens/classes that lack design-system backing.
common_pattern: SCSS/Tailwind styling conventions for typography in a design system: use design-system type-scale utilities/variants rather than ad-hoc font declarations, and scope styles to containers/component classes rather than element selectors. A separate naming sub-pattern (label1 vs label-1) contains a genuine contradiction and is excluded.

text: Validate packaging with `check-manifest` and run tests against the installed distribution, not just the source tree. Add `check-manifest` as a pre-commit hook (see the `torchbox/wagtailmedia` `.pre-commit-config.yaml` example) whenever `setup.py` filters packages with patterns like `find_packages(exclude=[...tests...])`, since manual include/exclude rules can silently omit required sub-packages or include unwanted files.
reason: Manual package include/exclude rules are fragile; local in-tree test runs may pass even when the shipped distribution is missing required files. Automated manifest validation catches missing or extra files before release.
common_pattern: Validate packaging/manifest integrity with check-manifest and installed-package tests to catch files silently omitted or wrongly included by setup.py package filters.

text: In packaging configuration, avoid broad `find_packages(exclude=...)` patterns such as `*tests*` that include and exclude parts of the same namespace. Separate project tests, reusable test infrastructure, and distributable code into distinct package trees/namespaces (for example top-level `tests/`, `{package}.tests` for project tests, and `{package}.test` or `{package}.testutils` for reusable distributed test utilities). If a test-utility subpackage must still be distributed, include it explicitly in `MANIFEST.in` via `graft` rather than relying on package-data side effects.
reason: Broad test-exclusion globs can silently omit nested subpackages or reusable test-infrastructure packages that third parties import. Distinct namespaces make package discovery and manifest configuration unambiguous and avoid fragile include/exclude conflicts within the same namespace.
common_pattern: Packaging configuration should not both include and exclude the same package namespace with broad test-exclusion globs; instead, project tests, reusable test infrastructure, and distributable package code should live in distinct package trees/namespaces so `find_packages(exclude=...)` can exclude project tests without dropping required test utilities.

text: In `package.json` npm scripts, wrap glob patterns passed to CLI tools in escaped double quotes (`\"...\"`) rather than single quotes or leaving them unquoted, and apply the same quoting convention consistently to all scripts using the same CLI or glob pattern.
reason: Escaped double quotes keep the JSON string valid and work across POSIX shells and Windows `cmd`, while single quotes or unquoted globs can be passed literally and behave inconsistently.
common_pattern: Cross-platform shell quoting convention for glob patterns in package.json npm scripts, plus consistency across analogous scripts.

text: Place subsystem-specific configuration types and loaders in the subsystem's existing dedicated config module (e.g., `config/{subsystem}Config.js`) instead of a generic utility config file, and keep a single configuration JSON script/source per subsystem rather than introducing a second config script or tag for the same subsystem.
reason: Multiple config scripts sharing the same conceptual name are confusing and can drift out of sync; a single, discoverable per-subsystem config module makes configuration easier to maintain.
common_pattern: Subsystem configuration should live in one dedicated config module per subsystem, avoiding duplicate or parallel config sources for the same subsystem.

text: In `.eslintrc.js` ESLint `member-ordering` overrides, configure `memberTypes` deliberately: order important but less common class members such as `signature` before common members like `field` and `method` (e.g. `['signature', 'field', 'method']`), and keep member-type inclusion consistent with the rest of the override—omit a type such as `constructor` when another rule disallows it, unless the project intentionally allows edge-case constructors and needs uniform ordering for them.
reason: Surfacing `signature` early makes class interfaces easier to inspect, while aligning `memberTypes` with other rules avoids internally contradictory ESLint configuration; retaining `constructor` is only justified when edge-case classes still need it or the rule may later apply consistently across all classes.
common_pattern: Configuring ESLint `member-ordering` `memberTypes` in `.eslintrc.js`, especially ordering important but uncommon member types (`signature`) early and keeping the member list consistent with other rules in the same override.

text: For cached data that must stay consistent across requests, threads, or long-lived worker processes — including cached model-derived values — use Django’s cache framework with a central, globally shared backend (e.g. Redis) rather than process/thread-local in-memory or module-local dict/LRU caches. Explicitly purge the relevant cache entries in the create/update flow of the source model so invalidation propagates reliably across processes and threads. If local caching is used, layer it with TTL-based expiry backed by a shared secondary cache so invalidation reaches all workers, and document that every application process must use the same cache instance/backend.
reason: Process-, thread-, and module-local caches cannot reliably invalidate each other, causing stale or inconsistent data across workers; a shared backend with explicit invalidation, or a layered TTL/local-plus-shared approach, improves consistency and cache hit rate for cross-request, high-read data.
common_pattern: Caching strategy consistency across process/thread boundaries: avoid process- or thread-local in-memory caches for data that must be shared, invalidatable, or high-hit-rate across long-lived workers; prefer a central shared cache or a layered cache with TTL/invalidation, and document that all workers must use the same backend.

text: Define controller/widget defaults centrally on the controller or its shared attribute helper, and let HTML/template callers omit data attributes/params that merely restate those defaults. Only expose optional overrides when there is a concrete reuse case and a clear sensible default; apply concrete behavior-specific values at the widget/usage level, and bind primary HTML configuration through the `value` attribute/property rather than params or event detail. When a UI element needs a fixed fallback value that must be independent of the current user selection (e.g., a fallback preview size), define it in the controller/JS logic rather than passing it through the template as a data attribute or coupling it to the template's default/selected state.
reason: Merged from two complementary rules about centralizing controller defaults and avoiding redundant or coupled template data attributes. Rule 107 provides the general convention for controller configuration and HTML binding; Rule 1918 specifies the case of fixed fallback values that must remain independent of user selection.
common_pattern: Controller/widget configuration should be declarative and minimal: sensible defaults live in the controller or shared attribute helper, callers omit attributes/params that merely restate those defaults, optional overrides are exposed only for concrete needs, and primary HTML configuration uses the declarative value attribute.

text: When an optional config key is missing and a default/fallback exists, handle it gracefully: fall back to the default (or no-op/preserve current state) rather than throwing, assuming presence, or logging a console.error — a default value makes the missing key expected, not an error. For optional mapping config, use `.get(key, {})` to handle absent keys. Note that `.get(key, {})` alone does not protect against an explicitly provided `None` (e.g., `dict.update(None)` will raise); decide deliberately per call site whether to coerce `None` to the fallback or allow fail-fast.
reason: Unguarded nested access on a missing optional config key throws runtime errors and regresses fallback behavior; logging errors for expected missing optional values creates noise. `.get(key, {})` defaults only when the key is absent, so a present `None` must be handled deliberately per call site.
scope: optional configuration keys and mapping fallbacks
common_pattern: Robust handling of optional/missing configuration keys: distinguishing 'absent' from 'present but invalid', and choosing graceful fallback/default behavior (or deliberate fail-fast) rather than unguarded nested access or noisy error logging.

text: Keep lint/format rules enabled by default and prefer linting/formatting all files. For necessary exceptions, use the narrowest scoped mechanism rather than global disables or broad ignores: configure file-local/scoped overrides (e.g. stylelint `overrides` with `files`; ESLint `overrides` with `files` globs aligned to supported file extensions, adding specific files to the central exemption array in `.eslintrc.js`; explicit path exclusions in `.semgrep.yml` for intentionally unfixed files) instead of weakening or removing rules globally; use scoped inline directives for localized code exceptions, but do not put formatter/linter inline ignore directives in user-facing templates such as `.github/` PR/issue templates—exclude those files via config instead. When config-level ignores are unavoidable, target the narrowest specific file/path, and do not document or encourage whole-file `ignoreFiles` mechanisms.
reason: Scoped exceptions keep rules enforced for unaffected files, avoid ever-growing exclusion lists, and prevent broad ignores from hiding issues across entire paths.
common_pattern: Minimizing lint and type-check suppressions: fix root causes first, scope unavoidable suppressions narrowly, and keep them documented and current.

text: When adopting, changing, or migrating a linter/formatter rule or config tool, configure the tool to match the project's existing conventions (preserve prior formatting such as `lines-after-imports`, override rules that produce false positives against domain vocabulary, set disruptive rules to non-blocking until contributors can satisfy them) rather than accepting widespread churn or requiring wholesale rewrites. Document the old-to-new rule-by-rule mapping for tool migrations in the PR description or comment (not inline in the committed config file) so reviewers can assess migration coverage and equivalence gaps.
reason: Keeps diffs focused on functional changes, avoids unrelated formatting noise, and makes migration parity auditable without leaving obsolete tool references in production config.
common_pattern: Managing the relationship between linter/formatter tooling and the existing codebase: how to configure rules that conflict with project conventions, how to resolve flags on the code side, and how to make tool migrations reviewable.

text: New rules added to `.semgrep.yml` must follow the existing rule structure: include an `id`, a descriptive `message`, applicable `languages`, a `severity`, and a pattern matching the prohibited construct. Message fields must be concrete and framework-agnostic: give a code-level remediation example (e.g. `element.classList.add/remove()` or `element.style.width = '200px'`) and suggest generic web-platform alternatives (CSS classes, data attributes) rather than framework-specific attribute names or vague phrasing like 'prefer ...', unless the rule is explicitly scoped to that framework. When adding a rule that bans one inline HTML mechanism (e.g. `style` attributes), add companion rules covering the other related inline constructs (e.g. `<style>` elements, `<script>` elements, `setAttribute('style', ...)`) so CSP-violating and inline-style patterns are enforced consistently without gaps.
reason: Consistency with existing Semgrep rules keeps enforcement predictable, while concrete, framework-neutral messages make custom lint rules self-documenting and broadly applicable.
common_pattern: Authoring and maintaining Semgrep rules in `.semgrep.yml`: rule messages must be concrete and framework-agnostic, new rules must follow the established `id`/`message`/`languages`/`severity`/`pattern` structure, enforcement coverage should be extended to companion constructs when banning a class of inline HTML patterns, and known out-of-scope violations should be handled with path exclusions rather than weakening the rule.

text: Keep test settings and CI coverage aligned with all supported database/search backends: retain or add `WAGTAILSEARCH_BACKENDS` entries for each backend (e.g. postgresql, mysql, sqlite) in test settings, and when CI runs against a specific search backend, include every test module parameterized by that backend (page search, documents, images, etc.), not just a subset.
reason: Ensures backend-parameterized tests exercise every supported backend and prevents backend-specific regressions in unlisted modules from being missed.
scope: wagtail/test/settings.py and CI workflows for search backend testing
common_pattern: Conventions for testing Wagtail's pluggable search backends: shared cross-backend tests stay backend-agnostic, backend-specific behavior and setup live in backend-specific test subclasses, and backends are configured/obtained through the real WAGTAILSEARCH_BACKENDS configuration path.

text: When integrating Axe-core include/exclude selectors, represent selector lists as arrays in your own configuration for consistency and multi-selector support, but normalize any incoming value before use by accepting both a string and an array (e.g., `Array.isArray` or wrap in an array); when building `fromFrames`/`fromShadowDom` frame context, join multiple selectors into a single comma-separated string rather than appending each selector as a separate array element.
reason: Arrays let Axe combine shadow DOM and regular selectors and keep related options consistent, while accepting string or array prevents runtime errors from documented/userbar configurations that may use plain strings. Axe treats each `fromFrames` array element except the last as a nested iframe target, so joining selectors avoids misinterpreting extra selectors as iframe names.
common_pattern: Handling Axe-core include/exclude selector configuration: prefer/normalize selector lists to arrays, and respect Axe's frame-context array semantics when building fromFrames/fromShadowDom.

text: Centralize custom Axe accessibility rules and checks in the shared configuration lists (`axe_custom_rules` / `axe_custom_checks`, defined in the shared `a11y-result` module) instead of as separate private attributes, per-rule fields, or client-side implementations. Extend the checker with additive configuration attributes (e.g. `axe_rules`) that compose with the primary selection filter (`axe_run_only`) rather than overloading a single option. When defining custom Axe rules/checks, set `enabled` to `False` in the rule definition and supply configurable values (e.g. regex patterns, as strings) via an `options` dict for the `axe.configure` API. Control execution through the run-only mechanism, and be aware that axe-core's `spec` overrides `runOnly`, so custom-rule enablement may need separate handling. Document that a falsy run-only value (e.g. `None`) omits `runOnly` and makes Axe run all non-experimental rules.
reason: Keeping all custom rules/checks in shared collections gives a single source of truth, avoids duplicated implementation across components, and lets every rule be discovered, overridden, and modified the same way. Additive config attributes keep distinct concerns (which rules run vs. toggling individual rules) separate. Setting `enabled: False` and using `options` matches the `axe.configure` API contract and existing rule configuration pattern, preventing custom rules/checks from being silently active or silently overridden, while documenting run-only behavior makes the checker's less-obvious behavior explicit.
scope: wagtail/admin/userbar.py AccessibilityItem and shared a11y-result module; AccessibilityItem rule/check definitions
common_pattern: Centralized, consistent configuration of the Axe accessibility checker: custom rules/checks should live in shared configuration collections rather than duplicate or dedicated attributes; per-rule enablement and options follow a single pattern; and accessibility test scopes/exclusions should stay accurate.

text: Reference Django apps by their fully qualified dotted path, and when an app defines a custom `AppConfig`, use the full config path (`{app}.apps.{AppConfig}Class`) in `INSTALLED_APPS` and in user-facing messages/documentation — not the bare app label or short name.
reason: Users configure and register apps by their full dotted path in settings, so code, warnings, and docs should reference the same identifier. This ensures custom `AppConfig` initialization hooks run, avoids ambiguity when short labels collide, and makes messages directly actionable.
common_pattern: Django AppConfig conventions: how apps are referenced (full dotted/config path vs. bare label) and where app-specific setup/label belongs (in the app's own AppConfig).

text: When adding or updating a linter/formatter pre-commit hook, explicitly set its `files`/`types`/`types_or` filters to match the exact file extensions the project intends to lint, rather than relying on the hook's default file matching.
reason: Pre-commit linter hooks often default to broad or limited file patterns; explicit filtering avoids processing unsupported files or silently skipping relevant files such as `.ts`/`.tsx`.
common_pattern: Best practices for `.pre-commit-config.yaml`: keep hook tool versions synchronized with project dependency manifests, explicitly scope hooks to the intended files, and prefer minimal/maintained/project-managed hook configuration.

text: Prefer minimal, maintained, project-managed pre-commit hook configuration: do not set `language_version` unless a non-default interpreter is required; prefer purpose-built maintained hook repositories; keep `additional_dependencies` minimal; and when a tool is already version-managed in `package.json`, use a local hook running the project's npm script instead of duplicating dependency pins.
reason: Reduces unnecessary configuration, avoids conflicting dependency sets, and leverages the project's existing toolchain instead of maintaining duplicate version declarations.
common_pattern: Best practices for `.pre-commit-config.yaml`: keep hook tool versions synchronized with project dependency manifests, explicitly scope hooks to the intended files, and prefer minimal/maintained/project-managed hook configuration.

text: Accessibility or content checks that must recognize any supported image file should match against Django's full list of valid image extensions (e.g. get_available_image_extensions() / the image extension validator), not Wagtail's configurable get_allowed_image_extensions() / WAGTAILIMAGES_EXTENSIONS, so images are not missed if the setting is later restricted or changed.
reason: get_allowed_image_extensions reflects current site configuration and may omit formats Wagtail can still support, causing false negatives in checks like the alt-text checker.
scope: `wagtail/admin/userbar.py` accessibility item checks; applies to image-detection logic that must remain stable across settings changes
common_pattern: Precise and consistent handling of image format/extension support in Wagtail: documentation must explicitly enumerate supported extensions, code lists/mappings must follow established conventions, and recognition checks must use the full set of supported image extensions rather than a configurable subset.

text: In GitHub Actions test workflows (e.g., `.github/workflows/test.yml`), avoid inflating the CI matrix with new entries, keys, or runner jobs. When adding coverage for a new dependency version, distribute that version across existing matrix combinations or replace a lower-priority job instead, and use `env`/conditional expressions for auxiliary per-job configuration rather than adding extra matrix keys.
reason: Extra matrix entries multiply jobs and CI resource usage, while extra matrix keys add noise to generated job names and check summaries. Existing combinations can usually provide sufficient coverage without increasing runner count or runtime.
common_pattern: GitHub Actions CI test matrix hygiene: keeping matrix configuration resource-efficient, accurately documented, and clearly representative of the jobs it defines.

text: In Django settings modules, apply environment-specific overrides via `settings/local.py` imported after overridable settings, and override individual nested keys rather than reassigning whole settings dictionaries; if a dictionary setting must be replaced, define every required key because Django does not merge dictionary settings with defaults.
reason: Django does not merge dictionary settings, and settings defined after the local import cannot be overridden by `local.py`; incorrect overrides can discard required defaults and defeat environment-specific configuration.
scope: Django settings modules and project templates
common_pattern: Correct handling and documentation of Django settings in project templates and docs: respect Django's settings override/merge semantics and make settings location, examples, and formatting explicit for users.

text: In project-template Dockerfiles, do not set `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE` or override settings defaults; rely on the values already defined by the generated project's `wsgi.py`/`manage.py` to keep the template unopinionated.
reason: Avoids imposing extra configuration opinions and duplicating settings that scaffolding already defines, which can drift or confuse users.
common_pattern: Correct handling and documentation of Django settings in project templates and docs: respect Django's settings override/merge semantics and make settings location, examples, and formatting explicit for users.

text: When a Wagtail setting maps to a Django formatting/localization option (e.g., WAGTAIL_DATE_FORMAT → DATE_INPUT_FORMATS), treat it as dependent on Django localization: add a system check that warns when the configured value is not among the effective Django formats, and when USE_L10N=True validate get_format() for every language allowed in user profiles (passing lang=), not only the current locale. Also document that non-default Wagtail format settings may require coordinating with Django locale/format settings.
reason: Prevents silent fallback to unexpected formats, catches misconfiguration for users with non-default language preferences, and reduces confusion for users overriding format settings without adjusting Django locale configuration.
common_pattern: Wagtail format settings that depend on Django localization must be validated and documented against Django's effective locale/format configuration, including USE_L10N and all languages allowed in user profiles.

text: After editing TypeScript frontend source under `client/src/controllers/`, recompile the frontend assets before relying on the change at runtime, because Wagtail serves compiled static assets rather than the TypeScript source directly.
reason: The runtime uses compiled static assets, so TypeScript controller edits are not usable until the frontend build is rerun.
common_pattern: Wagtail client-side code under `client/src/` is TypeScript-based: new front-end files should be authored in TypeScript, and TypeScript controller edits require recompilation into served frontend assets.

text: In Wagtail rich-text converter/handler registration, always-on default features must register rules for every relevant ruleset (e.g. both `contentstate` and `editorhtml`), following the rule structure used by neighbouring default features; optional/configurable features must not be embedded in the default ruleset and should instead register conditionally through their configuration or hook registration.
reason: Default features with incomplete ruleset coverage are silently stripped by consumers using the missing ruleset, breaking lossless round-trip behaviour; embedding optional handlers in the default ruleset enables features even when toggles should control them.
common_pattern: Default/always-on rich-text feature registration must be complete across all relevant rulesets, while optional/configurable features must be registered conditionally and excluded from the default ruleset.

text: Gate optional, feature-specific, or potentially costly code behind its enabling setting or feature flag with a safe default (e.g. `getattr(settings, "WAGTAIL_I18N_ENABLED", False)`). This includes model imports, admin filter registration, extra database queries, loops, and hooks. When the feature is disabled, do not import its models, register its feature-specific filters, or incur its performance penalties.
reason: Prevents loading feature-specific models, exposing feature-specific filters, and causing performance penalties or unintended behavior changes in projects where the feature is not configured or enabled.
common_pattern: Optional or potentially costly behavior should be gated behind a settings/feature flag so it only runs when explicitly enabled.

text: For django-treebeard tree models (e.g. Wagtail's `Collection`), define ordering via `Meta.node_order_by` (e.g. `node_order_by=['name']`) instead of applying `.order_by()` on individual querysets. Treebeard encodes `node_order_by` into the node path, so this keeps `get_children()`/`get_descendants()` ordering consistent. When broadening a query from `get_children()` to `get_descendants()`, preserve the existing ordering contract — do not silently substitute a different order (e.g. `.order_by('path')` for `.order_by('name')`) unless the change is intentional and regressions are handled via `node_order_by` or a data migration. When a model uses `node_order_by`, do not pass manual position arguments (e.g. `last-child`) as move targets.
reason: A single declarative ordering source prevents the ordering regressions that occur when tree-query scope and per-query `.order_by()` are changed together, and avoids conflicts between automatic and manual ordering.
scope: project-wide (Wagtail treebeard tree models, e.g. Collection)
common_pattern: Ordering behavior of django-treebeard tree models: define ordering declaratively via `node_order_by` at the model level rather than per-query `.order_by()`, preserve the established ordering contract when broadening traversal scope, and keep ordering-dependent tests in sync.

text: Add a database index on model fields that are used in frequently executed lookups or filters—such as suffix/`endswith` queries, save/upload duplicate checks, or middleware per-request checks—to avoid full-table scans.
reason: Without an index, these queries can scan many rows and degrade as tables grow, especially when run on every request or upload.
common_pattern: Django database index best practices: index performance-critical lookups, and name indexes explicitly with abstract-model-safe placeholders.

text: In `tailwind.config.js`, scope each `content` glob precisely to the source directories and file extensions that actually contain Tailwind utility class names, and avoid exclusions that inadvertently drop other code sources. Include only extensions actually used in each source tree and omit unused ones: for example, use `{html,js,ts,tsx}` (no `.jsx`, since React components are `.tsx`) for app/client globs; include `.py` for Wagtail app code that can define class strings via `./wagtail/**!(static)/*.{html,js,ts,tsx,py}`, keeping `!(static)` to avoid purging compiled assets; and use `{md,rst}` or `{html,js,ts,tsx,md,rst}` for `./docs/**` since documentation is authored in Markdown/reStructuredText. Extensions omitted from a glob have their classes purged, while extensions included but unused add needless scanning. When a `content` glob must exclude a directory to avoid rebuild loops (e.g. `client/scss`), do not narrow the glob to a single sibling directory like `client/src`; keep scanning the other code directories using a multi-directory glob such as `./client/{src,storybook,tests}/**/*.{js,ts,tsx,mdx}` or an exclusion pattern such as `./client/[!scss]/**/*.{js,ts,tsx,mdx}`.
reason: Tailwind's JIT builds output only from classes seen in the configured content globs. Missing real source extensions (e.g. `.md`/`.rst` for docs, `.py` for Wagtail code) purges classes that are actually used, unused extensions cause unnecessary work and config drift, and narrowing an exclusion to one sibling directory silently stops Tailwind from scanning other content sources such as Storybook and tests, purging their utility classes.
common_pattern: Tailwind `content` globs in tailwind.config.js must be kept tightly aligned with the actual source files: list the file extensions that really contain utility classes for each source tree, omit extensions the project doesn't use, and when excluding directories, do not narrow the glob to a single sibling directory.

text: In configuration files, prefer a format that supports comments (e.g., YAML over JSON) when inline comments are useful for documenting non-obvious configuration rules, rationale, caveats, or exceptions. Reserve inline comments for non-obvious rationale, caveats, or intentional behavior; avoid comments that duplicate default values/options, restate standard tool/config behavior, or document temporary workarounds. Update or remove comments when the referenced configuration state changes.
reason: Ensures configuration comments are both possible (via format choice) and purposeful, reducing drift and noise while keeping maintainers from being misled by stale or redundant explanations.
common_pattern: Hygiene for inline comments in configuration files: comments should be concise, accurate, and reserved for non-obvious rationale; avoid duplicating defaults/values, restating standard tool behavior, or documenting stale/temporary workarounds. A related sub-pattern is choosing a config format that supports comments when such documentation is needed.

text: In Sphinx documentation (`docs/conf.py` and theme templates), prefer built-in Sphinx configuration options and template variables (e.g., `root_doc`, `pagename`, `pathto()`) over custom `conf.py` variables or manually derived path variables; if a built-in covers the need, remove the custom variable. Specifically, define `source_suffix` explicitly as a dict mapping each supported file extension to its parser in `docs/conf.py` when that avoids warning logs or reliance on implicit parser-plugin registration. Use `pathto()` for links to generated pages rather than `root_doc` or custom base-path variables.
reason: Built-in Sphinx facilities are upstream-maintained, always available in template context, and eliminate redundant configuration that can drift, clutter `conf.py`, or resolve incorrectly. Explicit `source_suffix` configuration avoids unnecessary Sphinx logs during format migration and reduces reliance on implicit plugin behavior.
scope: Sphinx docs configuration (`docs/conf.py`) and theme templates
common_pattern: Sphinx/Read the Docs configuration and documentation hygiene: minimize redundant configuration by preferring built-in Sphinx facilities, document non-obvious config choices, and avoid duplicating documentation content across files.

text: When modifying `wagtail/embeds/oembed_providers.py`, keep provider definitions and registry entries in sync: remove deleted providers completely — including any associated definitions and references — and add every new provider dictionary to the `all_providers` list so it is actually registered.
reason: Removing only a list entry leaves orphaned definitions or dead code, while defining a provider without adding it to `all_providers` makes the provider inert and unregistered.
common_pattern: Maintenance consistency rules for the oEmbed provider registry in `wagtail/embeds/oembed_providers.py`: provider additions and removals must be complete, registry entries must be kept in sync with provider definitions, and the file's alphabetical ordering convention must be preserved.

text: Define transliteration maps in `client/src/utils/urlify.config.json` using locale-qualified `{LANGUAGE}_MAP:{locale}` keys (e.g., `RUSSIAN_MAP:ru`, `BELARUSIAN_MAP:be`). For each map, provide symmetric uppercase/lowercase entries for every letter, and omit characters that are not part of the target language's alphabet rather than including them as no-op mappings to an empty string.
reason: Locale-qualified keys disambiguate closely related languages, symmetric case pairs prevent incorrect slugs depending on input casing, and redundant no-op entries for non-alphabet characters (e.g., `["Ъ", ""]`) add noise and can leak across adapted language maps.
common_pattern: Conventions for defining and maintaining language transliteration maps in the project's urlify configuration (client/src/utils/urlify.config.json): consistent key naming/case handling, standards compliance, and locale fallback behavior.

text: When a language has an official transliteration standard (e.g., GOST 7.0-2014 for Russian), transliteration map values must conform to that standard for both lowercase and uppercase characters; for characters with multiple valid outputs, align with the referenced standard or document the chosen alternative. When fixing one language's map, audit related language maps (e.g., Belarusian, Ukrainian) for the same standard-compliance issues and handle language-specific alphabet differences explicitly rather than inheriting from a sibling language's map.
reason: Standards compliance ensures correct, consistent, and interoperable slugs; leaving related locales unaudited or inheriting another language's map causes the same class of transliteration errors to persist and mis-transliterates language-unique letters.
common_pattern: Conventions for defining and maintaining language transliteration maps in the project's urlify configuration (client/src/utils/urlify.config.json): consistent key naming/case handling, standards compliance, and locale fallback behavior.

text: For locales with incomplete transliteration maps, `urlify` should prioritize the requested locale's map and fall back to a related locale's mapping (e.g., Russian for Belarusian) for characters missing from the primary locale.
reason: Matches real-world multilingual usage (e.g., Belarus uses both Russian and Belarusian officially) and avoids broken transliteration for unmapped characters.
common_pattern: Conventions for defining and maintaining language transliteration maps in the project's urlify configuration (client/src/utils/urlify.config.json): consistent key naming/case handling, standards compliance, and locale fallback behavior.

text: Steps in `.github/workflows/*.yml` that must run on pull requests from forks must not require repository secrets (fork PR runners only receive `GITHUB_TOKEN`). Use tokenless auth paths, guard secret-dependent steps with conditions so they tolerate an empty/unset secret (e.g., set `fail_ci_if_error: false`), and, for Codecov uploads without the official `codecov-action@v4+` (e.g., Codecov CLI or another action), construct an unprotected branch name for PR builds (e.g., prefix with `pr-<pr-number>:` or `<fork-author>:`) to enable tokenless uploads; store `CODECOV_TOKEN` in CI project environment variables (not config files) for protected-branch uploads.
reason: GitHub Actions does not pass repository secrets (except `GITHUB_TOKEN`) to runners for workflows triggered from forked repositories, so any secret-backed configuration silently fails on fork PR builds. Codecov in particular only accepts tokenless uploads when the repo is public and the branch is unprotected; `codecov-action@v4+` adds the required branch prefix automatically, but other setups must do it manually, and protected branches still need a real token supplied securely via CI env vars.
common_pattern: CI workflows that run on forked PRs must not depend on repository secrets, since GitHub Actions withholds them; this general principle drives both the tokenless-upload configuration for coverage tools (Codecov) and the fallback of pinning action versions when an upgrade breaks fork-PR runs.

text: For Python Dockerfiles (especially `wagtail/project_template/Dockerfile`), avoid Alpine-based Python images because musl libc causes slow builds and missing prebuilt wheels; prefer Debian-based Python images. Use a `-slim` variant by default, but choose the full non-slim Debian image (e.g. `python:<version>-buster`) when the Dockerfile needs native build dependencies such as Pillow, mysqlclient, or psycopg2, or when installing packages would otherwise pull in a competing Debian Python runtime/larger final image.
reason: Alpine reduces size at the cost of Python build compatibility and speed, while full Debian images are unnecessarily large unless native build tooling is required. Selecting the right variant avoids both slow builds and duplicated build-dependency installation.
common_pattern: Dockerfile configuration for Python/Wagtail project templates: base image selection and layer/dependency optimization

text: Pin the underlying distribution version in Docker base image tags (e.g. `python:3.6-stretch` rather than `python:3.6`) instead of using floating language-version-only tags.
reason: Pinning the OS release makes builds reproducible and avoids surprise breakages when the upstream base image is updated.
common_pattern: Dockerfile configuration for Python/Wagtail project templates: base image selection and layer/dependency optimization

text: Define registry instances once in a central module and import that shared instance wherever needed, instead of instantiating a new registry at each use site or locally in other modules such as template tags.
reason: Avoids duplicate registration/scanning work, prevents divergent registry state, and keeps behavior consistent with existing central registry singletons.
common_pattern: Registry design conventions: use descriptive domain-specific registry names, define a single shared registry instance in a central module and import it, and keep registry classes limited to configuration collection rather than domain logic.

text: Sort keys/properties alphabetically in configuration objects, class/object property declarations, and framework value maps (e.g. `tsconfig.json` `compilerOptions` and Stimulus `static values`/`targets`), and in manually maintained lists such as provider entries in `wagtail/embeds/oembed_providers.py`. Insert new entries in sorted position rather than appending, and document the ordering convention for manually maintained lists, unless the tool's official documentation or a functional requirement dictates another order.
reason: Alphabetical ordering improves scanability, makes options/properties/providers easier to locate and compare, reduces diff churn and merge conflicts, and keeps shared configuration, controller definitions, and provider lists consistent across contributors.
common_pattern: Alphabetical ordering of keys, properties, and entries in configuration objects, code declarations, and framework value maps to improve scanability, consistency, and merge-conflict reduction.

text: Extract shared behavior instead of duplicating bodies. When two implementations differ only by a small variation (a single flag, parameter value, or strategy class), move the shared behavior into a common helper or shared method with a parameterized difference and have the variants delegate to it. For admin widgets and parallel forms (e.g. images/documents upload forms, all consumers of a shared widget), put the shared logic in a single behavior-named shared location—a dedicated JS module/file (e.g. `collapsible.js`), shared widget/base class, or mixin—and reference it from every place that needs it rather than duplicating across templates, per-template inline scripts, `static_src` files, or a single model's form. Mirror the same widget/controller configuration across every parallel form/consumer that uses the shared widget so they stay in sync. Keep form-internals-specific code next to the form that owns it; only genuinely form-agnostic helpers belong in shared admin core utilities. Avoid the opposite extreme: do not replace small page-specific inline scripts with a broad shared bundle that pulls in substantial unused functionality.
reason: Duplicated bodies drift apart over time and force the same fix to be applied in multiple places. A single shared source of truth for reusable widget/JS behavior prevents drift across sibling forms and keeps behavior in sync, while preserving clean separation between form-specific and shared admin code without over-bundling.
scope: Global DRY/shared-behavior extraction; Wagtail admin widgets/parallel media-type forms and shared admin JavaScript modules
common_pattern: Refactoring guidance on when and how to compose/decompose code: eliminate near-duplicate implementations by sharing a helper or parameterizing the variation, decompose unwieldy methods into focused helpers along responsibility boundaries — while resisting premature fragmentation — and rename helpers that have been decoupled from their former context.

text: Reuse rather than recompute: when the same expression, lookup, or derived value is needed more than once (repeated branches, loop iterations, repeated comparisons, dictionary lookups with key conversion, or DOM queries), compute it once into a named local variable (or cache it) and reference that variable at each use site; conversely, do not introduce a temporary variable for a value used only once — inline the expression directly at its use site. Store DOM query results and reuse them rather than re-running the same query: consolidate an element's lookup and related manipulation into a single place (e.g., one function) and look elements up directly instead of scanning/filtering sibling collections inside a loop. Cache derived values and accessor-method results, especially inside render methods, repeatedly-invoked callbacks, and per-element loops, so the value is not recomputed and stays consistent across all uses; re-invoking accessor methods is acceptable only on cold paths where the call is cheap.
reason: A single derived value provides one source of truth so repeated logic cannot drift out of sync during refactors, and it avoids redundant work (duplicate queries, conversions, lookups, DOM scans, and recomputation in hot paths). Inlining single-use values removes unnecessary noise and indirection, keeping simple code compact.
common_pattern: Variable hygiene: introduce a named local variable when a value/expression is used more than once, and inline it when it is used only once — i.e. name things only when they earn their keep by being reused.

text: Write developer-facing console/error and user-facing check messages as complete sentences with consistent trailing punctuation (usually ending with a full stop to match surrounding module messages), and wrap code identifiers such as event names in backticks. In Django check functions, explicitly import any Django symbols used in the function scope (e.g. `settings`, `VERSION`) to avoid NameError; apply the check-specific message conventions in modules such as `wagtail/admin/checks.py`.
reason: Improves readability and consistency of developer- and user-facing messages, and ensures Django symbols are available in check functions.
common_pattern: Conventions for authoring and registering Wagtail/Django system checks: how check functions and their IDs/names should be written, documented, and kept stable.

text: Initialize or update UI components at the lifecycle/handler point where required DOM elements, UI state, and component state are already available; do not use arbitrary delays such as setTimeout or async completion callbacks to work around readiness or race conditions. In React, place programmatic DOM side effects that are consequences of state changes (e.g., focusing an element after a menu opens) inside a useEffect keyed on the relevant state rather than in event handlers with setTimeout.
reason: Timing-dependent initialization causes visual flashes, delayed feedback, redundant checks, and race-condition-prone bugs. Keeping DOM side effects in React's effect lifecycle synchronizes them with state changes and avoids arbitrary timing hacks.
scope: global (with React function component / frontend guidance)
common_pattern: UI/component initialization and state updates should occur at the correct lifecycle or handler point when required DOM elements, state, and UI readiness are already available, rather than relying on arbitrary delays such as setTimeout or delayed async completion callbacks.

text: When associating visible or supplementary text with a UI element, form control, region, menu, panel, or action, give the text/labelling element a stable `id` and reference it from the target element using `aria-describedby` for help, warning, status, or supplementary context, or `aria-labelledby` for primary visible labels. Derive both IDs from a single canonical identifier source. For Wagtail admin help text, use the existing `-helptext` (hyphen) suffix convention rather than Django's `_helptext` (underscore) form. In tests, assert that the referenced element exists and has the expected text content.
reason: Ensures assistive technologies can announce the appropriate label or description, prevents broken or mismatched ARIA references, catches regressions where the referenced element is missing or has incorrect text, and keeps ID naming consistent across admin rendering paths.
common_pattern: Accessibility association: link descriptive UI text (help, warning, status) to its control via the `aria-describedby` attribute and a matching element `id`, and use a consistent hyphenated id suffix (`-helptext`) for help text in Wagtail admin.

text: When composing a string (e.g. a CSS classname or a user-facing message) from multiple optional fragments, accumulate the fragments in a list and join them (e.g. `" ".join(fragments)`), or use a single f-string followed by `.strip()`. Do not branch separately on each optional value or each present/absent combination, and do not extract a helper method solely to format/concatenate the fragments.
reason: Avoids combinatorial conditional branching as optional pieces grow, removes duplicated fixed fragments, avoids stray leading/trailing whitespace, and prevents unnecessary abstraction.
common_pattern: String composition from optional/multiple fragments should be done linearly (list + join, or single f-string + strip) rather than via conditional branching per combination or via a dedicated helper method.

text: In Django templates, compose conditional CSS class lists via a reusable `classnames` simple_tag (filters falsy args, joins truthy ones with single spaces) rather than chaining `yesno` filters or inline `{% if %}` fragments; when a conditional filter must be used, apply it to the dynamic value (e.g. `value|yesno:'...'`) and keep spacing outside the filter arguments, not inside them.
reason: Inline conditionals and `yesno` arguments produce stray/double/missing whitespace (or concatenated names like `headerhasform`) that has repeatedly broken snapshot and unit tests; a single helper centralizes and normalizes class rendering.
common_pattern: Conventions for authoring CSS `class` attributes in Django templates: keep class strings normalized (no stray/duplicate whitespace, omit empty attributes), and compose conditional class lists through a reusable helper rather than inline `yesno`/`{% if %}` interpolation.

text: Prefer TypeScript/TSX for React source files. In Wagtail, author new front-end files under `client/src/` — including new components under `client/src/components/` — as `.ts`/`.tsx` rather than `.js`/`.jsx`. Exclude `.jsx` from relevant file globs/tooling, and omit `import React from 'react';` in `.tsx`/`.jsx` files when the project uses the automatic JSX runtime and React APIs are not otherwise used.
reason: Using TypeScript from the start provides type safety and avoids later JS-to-TS migration/refactoring. Excluding `.jsx` from tooling and avoiding unused React imports reduces noise and linting errors under the automatic JSX runtime.
scope: Wagtail front-end React code, especially new files under `client/src/` and `client/src/components/`; project-wide React source files for `.jsx` globs/tooling and automatic JSX runtime imports
common_pattern: Wagtail client-side code under `client/src/` is TypeScript-based: new front-end files should be authored in TypeScript, and TypeScript controller edits require recompilation into served frontend assets.

text: Align or center icons and similar small leading/inline elements—including the Wagtail admin header avatar—using flexbox/component layout on the parent wrapper rather than `position: absolute` on the element itself. For icon-only controls, make the hit area square (equal width/height or `aspect-ratio`) and center the icon with flex, avoiding asymmetric padding. In the Wagtail admin header, lay out the avatar and welcome text via component layout: apply flex utilities on `<header>` (e.g. `w-flex`, or a `header--with-avatar` modifier) and/or add alignment rules to `client/scss/components/_header.scss`; for optical alignment prefer a negative logical margin (e.g. `margin-inline-start`) over absolute offsets such as `left: -70px`, tuning the value visually to preserve RTL. Any template change that adds an element inside the header `h1` must ship matching component SCSS or it renders in the wrong position.
reason: Flexbox/component layout keeps elements in normal document flow, avoids absolute-positioning side effects and magic offsets/RTL breakage, fixes misalignment at the layout-container level, and yields a balanced, predictable hit target.
scope: CSS/SCSS component styles for icons and icon wrappers; Wagtail admin header (`client/scss/components/_header.scss` and home header template)
common_pattern: Icon alignment/centering in CSS: prefer keeping elements in normal flow via flexbox alignment on the parent container over absolutely positioning the icon child; when absolute positioning is unavoidable, choose offset values that hold across component states and keep independent values separate.

text: Prefer built-in functions over directly invoking dunder/magic methods for standard operations. Use `setattr(obj, name, value)` and `getattr(obj, name)` instead of `obj.__setattr__(...)` or `obj.__getattribute__(...)` when dynamically accessing attributes by name, and use `str(obj)` instead of `obj.__str__()` when obtaining an object's string representation.
reason: Built-in functions are idiomatic, readable, and respect the normal object protocol without exposing internal implementation hooks at call sites. For string conversion they behave identically to the dunder call, but `str()` is clearer about intent.
common_pattern: Use built-in attribute accessor functions (`setattr`/`getattr`) instead of calling dunder methods (`__setattr__`/`__getattribute__`) directly when accessing attributes dynamically by name.

text: When a compatibility fix, pattern change, or shared UI control/render-path migration (e.g., converting an inline action to a button or changing an icon approach) is cross-cutting, apply it to every affected occurrence — all call sites, backends, backend versions, version-specific tests, and all usages/shared render paths — not just the single instance where the issue was first reported. This preserves visual and behavioral consistency and avoids partial migrations.
reason: The same incompatibility or outdated pattern generally exists in all parallel code paths; fixing only the reported instance leaves the codebase inconsistent and the migration/issue partially unresolved.
common_pattern: Handling cross-cutting compatibility issues correctly: verify the problem is real against actual supported implementations, then apply the resulting fix consistently to every affected location/version rather than only the instance where it was first noticed.

text: Keep parallel rich-text whitelister implementations in sync: when changing link/embed handling in `DbHtmlInputWhitelister` (`wagtail/admin/rich_text/converters/db_html.py`), mirror the equivalent branch in `DbWhitelister` (`wagtail/admin/rich_text/converters/editor_html.py`) and vice versa.
reason: Database-format and editor-format input share sanitization semantics; divergence can leave a security gap in one path while the other remains fixed.
common_pattern: Rich-text link/HTML sanitization should use positive allowlists (including an `undefined$` escape for optional attributes) and keep parallel whitelister implementations aligned.

text: Centralize shared state and rendering: in `wagtail/contrib/redirects/views.py`, avoid duplicating state and rendering across branches—render `wagtailredirects/choose_import_file.html` from a single location instead of separate `render()` calls in the GET/no-POST and POST branches. Define canonical lists of supported/default upload formats (and similar option sets) once as module-level constants, class/static attributes, or a central mapping (e.g., expose `SUPPORTED_FORMATS` at module level rather than defining it locally inside `start_import`), then reference the same definitions in all view branches, forms, templates, tests, and management commands instead of embedding them in view logic.
reason: Centralizing the HTML render and the supported-formats list makes the `start_import` view's control flow clearer, creates a single discoverable source of truth, and keeps GET/POST branches and UI/CLI surfaces consistent, preventing untested or divergent format sets from being exposed.
common_pattern: Canonical option/format lists should be centralized as module-level constants or class/static attributes and reused across view branches, UI, forms, tests, and CLI/management commands rather than embedded in local view logic.

text: Remove debug/scratch artifacts before committing: ad-hoc debug output (e.g., console.log, print, pdb.set_trace, debug-only branches) and commented-out debug/scratch code. Use the project's logging facilities for any diagnostics that must remain; version control already preserves history so commented-out code is unnecessary. In Python library/module code, also remove leftover debug print statements; when output is intended, use print(...) function-call syntax, and for modules that must support both Python 2 and Python 3, include `from __future__ import print_function` at the top of the file.
reason: Leftover debug statements and commented-out code pollute stdout/console, can leak internal data or temporary/incomplete logic, cannot be controlled by log levels, add noise, become stale, reduce readability, and signal incomplete work — a common review-blocking artifact. Bare Python 2 print statement syntax breaks Python 3 compatibility, and without the future import a print(...) call is not true function-call syntax in Python 2.
scope: global; for Python 2/3-compatible modules, include the future import for intended print(...) calls
common_pattern: Remove development-only debugging artifacts (ad-hoc print/console statements, debugger calls, and commented-out debug/scratch code) before committing so shipped code contains only intentional, controlled output.

text: Choose data-access primitives by contract and intended fallback semantics. For optional attributes or mapping keys, prefer a single `getattr(obj, attr, default)` / `dict.get(key, fallback)` over `hasattr`/membership checks, `try`/`except`, or duplicated fallback branches, supplying the default once. Use direct `obj.attr` / `d[key]` when the attribute/key is guaranteed by an API/helper contract (fail fast on violation), and do not use `getattr(obj, 'attr')` without a default merely as defensive access. Only in performance-sensitive hot paths where the key is almost always present may you prefer `try`/`except KeyError` around direct indexing over `.get()` plus a `None` check. Choose the fallback form by semantics: pass the fallback as `getattr`'s default when only a missing attribute should fall back; use `getattr(obj, attr, None) or fallback` when both missing and falsy/None values should fall back, provided the attribute name is a valid string. For optional dict keys, use `d.get(key)` or `d.get(key, fallback)` rather than an if/else membership check or `try`/`except KeyError` with a simple default.
reason: Unifies attribute and dictionary access style: required vs optional vs hot-path reads, avoiding duplicated fallback logic while preserving fail-fast behavior for contract-guaranteed keys and the performance exception for hot paths.
scope: Python attribute and dictionary/key access where the value may be absent, guaranteed by contract, or read in a performance-sensitive hot path
common_pattern: Python optional-attribute access idioms: use `getattr` with a default for optional attributes/keys, direct attribute access for guaranteed attributes, and validate/resolve the attribute-name argument before calling `getattr`.

text: Keep a strict separation between JavaScript behavior hooks and CSS styling hooks: use `data-*` attributes as JavaScript behavior hooks only and never as CSS selectors; reserve `class` for styling. In client-side JavaScript, select DOM elements for behavior using dedicated, stable `data-*` attribute selectors (e.g. `[data-form-side]`, `header [data-w-slim-header-buttons]`) rather than CSS class selectors, IDs, DOM-structure selectors (e.g. `ul > li > a`), or generic tag selectors (e.g. `li`) and stacked negative class filters. Prefer explicit, robust selectors (data-* attributes, known stable IDs, existing global references, or state pseudo-classes such as `:not(.deleted)`) so that HTML structure or tag changes don't break interactions, and update the corresponding JS selector constants accordingly. Fall back to a class/ID or element selector (or scope to a stable container) only when no suitable `data-*` hook is practical, treat that as a documented deviation, and when a selector must be built from a class that has a shared constant, interpolate the constant (e.g. `.${DEFAULT_CLASS}`) rather than hardcoding the literal.
reason: Decouples JavaScript behavior from styling and markup: class names, tag names, and DOM hierarchy are presentation concerns that may be refactored, so coupling JS to them makes behavior fragile. Conversely, using data-* attributes in CSS breaks the separation of concerns because data attributes signal JS ownership while classes are the intended CSS styling hooks. Explicit hooks make JS ownership clear, stable, and self-documenting.
common_pattern: Frontend selector conventions: use `data-*` attributes as JavaScript behavior hooks and reserve CSS classes exclusively for styling (with the complementary rule that `data-*` attributes must not be used as CSS selectors).

text: For multi-key sorting, prefer a single `sorted()` call with a key function returning a tuple ordered by priority, rather than chaining multiple `sorted()` calls. For tuple components that need descending order in an otherwise ascending sort, negate or wrap those components inline; do not rely on the whole-call `reverse` flag. When constructing sort keys, use key components whose comparison semantics directly express the intended ordering: coerce presence-only fields to booleans (negating them for descending order) instead of comparing irrelevant raw values, and when forcing records to the front/back, use sentinel values guaranteed to sort before/after all real field values (e.g. `Value('')` for text fields) rather than arbitrary sentinels like `'-1'`.
reason: A single tuple key makes sort priority explicit, avoids reliance on stable-sort passes, keeps mixed directions local to the field that needs them, and prevents ordering bugs caused by comparing values that do not affect the intended order or by sentinels that may not reliably sort outside the real value range.
common_pattern: Sort keys should express the intended ordering through values whose comparison semantics are meaningful and guaranteed, rather than relying on incidental raw value comparisons or arbitrary sentinels.

text: Order collections deterministically by deriving a per-item sort key directly (e.g., the DOM position of each item's earliest target node) instead of building auxiliary arrays and index maps, and when items lack an explicit key, fall back to a stable default such as alphabetical order rather than requiring explicit registration.
reason: Explicit per-item key computation removes unnecessary intermediate state (`selectorIndex`, `getMinIndex`, index maps) and extra passes over nested data, keeping ordering logic clear; a deterministic fallback guarantees stable output for unregistered items so custom ordering registration stays optional.
common_pattern: Predictable/deterministic ordering of collections: how sort keys are derived, how ties or unregistered items are broken, and whether declared order is preserved for order-sensitive dispatch.

text: When clearing caches, mutate the existing cache object rather than rebinding it: call `dict.clear()` (or an existing cache-specific clearing method) instead of reassigning the global/shared cache to a new empty container, and reuse existing per-cache clearing methods instead of calling `.clear()` directly on underlying stores.
reason: Mutating preserves object identity so all modules holding references to the cache see the invalidation, and delegating to existing cache-clearing methods centralizes invalidation logic so future behavior changes apply consistently.
common_pattern: Correct cache-clearing idiom: invalidate caches by mutating the existing cache objects (preserving identity and centralizing logic) rather than rebinding globals or bypassing existing cache-specific clearing methods.

text: Group related form controls with semantic `<fieldset>` and `<legend>` elements (the legend may be visually hidden) instead of visual-only wrappers, headings, or a `<label>`, to provide an accessible group name.
reason: Gives assistive technology proper context for a group of controls and separates form structure from presentation.
common_pattern: Accessible HTML form semantics: properly associating labels with individual controls and using fieldset/legend for control groups.

text: When `@typescript-eslint/no-use-before-define` is triggered, reorder the code so the referenced function or const is declared before its first use instead of adding an `eslint-disable-next-line` (or similar) suppression comment. Prefer this reordering for both function declarations and handler/const declarations.
reason: Avoids unnecessary lint suppressions, keeps the rule enforcing real ordering/initialization issues, and makes dependencies and code readability clearer.
common_pattern: When `@typescript-eslint/no-use-before-define` fires, reorder the declaration (move it before its first reference) rather than adding an `eslint-disable-next-line` suppression.

text: Match the check to the value's semantic type: use direct truthiness for boolean flags/values (e.g. `if value:`, `if enabled:`), and use explicit presence checks (`is None`, `!== null`) when testing for absence. Do not use `!!` where truthiness already applies, and do not use a truthiness check when you mean 'is absent'.
reason: Truthiness and presence are different questions; conflating them (e.g. `if not value:` for `None`, or `!!x` in an already-boolean context) hides the real condition and can silently treat other falsy values as absent (or vice versa).
common_pattern: Handling of booleans and presence checks: choosing the check form that matches the value's semantic type (boolean vs. null/absence), guaranteeing boolean-typed return values and flags, and avoiding redundant or misleading coercions (`!!`, `is True`, `1`/`0`).

text: Treat DOM attributes that may contain multiple space-separated tokens (e.g. data-controller, data-action, class-like data attributes) as token lists: append a token by joining non-empty existing values with spaces, and query/select tokens with the CSS `~=` operator instead of exact `=`.
reason: Using explicit token-list construction avoids duplicated conditional string logic, and `~=` matching avoids missing elements when the attribute contains additional tokens.
common_pattern: Correct handling of space-separated token lists in DOM attributes and CSS attribute selectors: building token values safely, querying by token membership, and quoting dynamic selector values.

text: When constructing dynamic CSS attribute selectors, use template literals and quote the dynamic attribute value, e.g. `[data-${attribute}="${value}"]`.
reason: Template literals are more readable than string concatenation, and quoting the dynamic value prevents invalid selectors when the value contains spaces or special characters.
common_pattern: Correct handling of space-separated token lists in DOM attributes and CSS attribute selectors: building token values safely, querying by token membership, and quoting dynamic selector values.

text: When mutating DOM element attributes, keep each change explicit and targeted: process independent attributes in their own sequential read-transform-write blocks, and when iterating a collection, guard the write with an ID/selector check so non-matching elements are left unchanged.
reason: This combines the cluster's two complementary concerns: avoiding precomputed, entangled attribute updates and preventing collection-based mutations from clobbering non-target elements.
common_pattern: DOM attribute mutations should be explicit, localized, and applied only to the intended element.

text: For HTML attributes that contain JSON, wrap example attribute values in single quotes so inner double quotes need not be escaped, and in test fixtures interpolate `JSON.stringify(value)` instead of writing a manually escaped JSON literal. When documenting widget-provided attributes, state that the widget handles escaping automatically for standard usage but that manually constructing the attribute requires correct quoting.
reason: Prevents quoting/escaping mistakes in documentation and tests, and keeps fixture values tied to the actual data under assertion.
scope: HTML examples and test fixtures that place JSON into data attributes
common_pattern: Correct HTML attribute serialization and escaping in documentation examples and test fixtures, especially for JSON-valued and valueless/empty attributes.

text: Use the idiomatic emptiness check appropriate to the language: in Python, prefer truthiness (`if not collection:`) over `len(collection) == 0`; in JavaScript, do not rely on truthiness for arrays (empty arrays are always truthy) — use `.length > 0`, or `array && array.length > 0` when the value may be null/undefined. Use truthiness for optional collection properties where absence and emptiness are equivalent. Reserve explicit length comparisons for cases where the exact count matters (e.g., `len(x) == 1`, `len(x) > 1`), since truthiness only distinguishes empty from non-empty and cannot detect thresholds.
reason: The cluster converges on choosing language-appropriate emptiness idioms while warning that truthiness is insufficient for count/threshold checks. The apparent JS-vs-Python tension resolves as language-specific guidance, not contradiction.
common_pattern: Idiomatic collection emptiness/existence checks: prefer concise, language-appropriate constructs (Python truthiness, `any()` generators) over verbose manual patterns (`len() == 0`, explicit loops with `break`, intermediate lists), while using explicit length checks only when the actual count/threshold matters — not mere emptiness.

text: For existence checks over a collection, use a single-pass `any(<condition> for <item> in <collection>)` generator expression instead of an explicit loop with `break`, an intermediate filtered list, or a chain of per-key `not dict[key]` checks. Combine the filtering conditions inline so the predicate and the existence test live together.
reason: Four generalizations across three PRs all converge on replacing manual iteration/intermediate structures with `any()` generator expressions, including the `not any(dict.values())` case for dict emptiness.
common_pattern: Idiomatic collection emptiness/existence checks: prefer concise, language-appropriate constructs (Python truthiness, `any()` generators) over verbose manual patterns (`len() == 0`, explicit loops with `break`, intermediate lists), while using explicit length checks only when the actual count/threshold matters — not mere emptiness.

text: Do not use assignment expressions inside object literals or argument lists to pass a value; read the existing value and perform any intentional mutation as a separate statement.
reason: Inline assignment hides a side effect, can accidentally mutate configuration/state (e.g. updating a controller flag while constructing an object), and obscures what value is actually being passed.
common_pattern: Policies about when object destructuring should/shouldn't be used (explicit property access vs. destructuring, single vs. multi-property), plus the closely related anti-pattern of side-effecting assignment expressions inside object literals.

text: In HTML templates, avoid `target="_blank"` unless there is a strong, specific justification. When a link does open in a new tab, include `rel="noopener noreferrer"` (not just `noopener`) to protect against reverse tabnabbing in browsers that ignore `noopener`; do not include these `rel` attributes on links that open in the same tab.
reason: New-tab behavior overrides user browsing preferences and can create accessibility issues, while `target="_blank"` links without proper `rel` values expose the opener window to reverse tabnabbing in older browsers. `noreferrer` provides a fallback when `noopener` is ignored.
common_pattern: HTML link conventions for new-tab navigation: avoid `target="_blank"` unless justified, and when it is used, include `rel="noopener noreferrer"` to prevent reverse tabnabbing; do not carry those `rel` attributes on same-tab links.

text: Use one-shot registration (jQuery `.one()` or `addEventListener(..., { once: true })`) for handlers that should fire only once, and scope per-instance listeners to the specific element rather than `document` so `{ once: true }` works for every instance.
reason: One-shot registration auto-removes the listener, preventing leaks and re-triggering; a document-level `{ once: true }` listener only fires for the first instance, forcing fragile guard logic instead of clean per-instance initialization.
common_pattern: DOM event listener lifecycle management: attach listeners with stable, removable references and always detach them at the appropriate teardown, using one-shot registration when the handler should only fire once.

text: In `.scss` files, use Sass `//` comments for single-line comments; reserve CSS `/* ... */` block comments for cases where the comment must span multiple lines. Blank-line spacing rules that apply to block comments do not apply to `//` comments.
reason: Sass comments are removed during compilation and match the project's preferred style; `//` and `/* */` follow different formatting conventions, so block-comment spacing rules must not be applied to `//` comments.
common_pattern: SCSS/CSS stylesheet formatting conventions: whitespace hygiene (no trailing-whitespace-only or stray blank lines), comment syntax and placement, and keeping comments visually bound to the code they document.

text: When a CSS selector/condition list is documented by ordered comments, keep the code order identical to the comment order.
reason: Makes it easier to map each code condition to its documented rationale and reduces review/maintenance mistakes when exclusions are added or reordered.
common_pattern: SCSS/CSS stylesheet formatting conventions: whitespace hygiene (no trailing-whitespace-only or stray blank lines), comment syntax and placement, and keeping comments visually bound to the code they document.

text: When deferring a UI state change with a timer, store the timeout ID and call `clearTimeout` before scheduling a new one or when the related state is changed/reopened, so stale callbacks cannot fire against superseded state. Also check class/condition availability before scheduling the timer rather than inside the callback, and avoid defining controller methods named after browser globals (e.g. `setTimeout`) — call `window.setTimeout`/`window.clearTimeout` explicitly.
reason: Prevents race conditions where a delayed callback hides/mutates UI after the user already reopened or changed it, avoids unnecessary timers, and avoids shadowing/confusion with globals.
common_pattern: Managing asynchronous timing in client-side Stimulus/UI controllers: replacing fixed setTimeout/debounce delays with transition-aware helpers, and explicitly managing timer lifecycle (store ID, clear before rescheduling) so stale callbacks cannot fire against outdated UI state.

text: Use ES6 template literals for string interpolation and dynamic string construction; reserve `+` for arithmetic only. Do not wrap static strings or already-string values in template literals when no interpolation is needed.
reason: This merged rule captures the complementary halves of the cluster: template literals are the preferred way to build strings containing dynamic values, while unnecessary template literals add noise and obscure intent. `+` should remain unambiguous as arithmetic.
common_pattern: JavaScript string-construction style: prefer template literals for interpolation and dynamic string composition instead of `+` concatenation, reserve `+` for arithmetic, and avoid unnecessary template literals when there is no interpolation or when passing an already-string value directly.

text: Use ES6 object property shorthand (`{ key }` instead of `{ key: key }`) when a property key matches an in-scope variable or parameter name; when writing function parameters that populate an object literal, name the parameter to match the target property key so shorthand can be used.
reason: Redundant `key: key` assignments reduce readability; aligning parameter/variable names with the resulting data shape enables idiomatic, concise object literals.
common_pattern: Prefer ES6 object property shorthand by aligning names — either the local variable/parameter name should match the property key, or the property key should be written using shorthand when an identically-named in-scope variable exists.

text: Break complex expressions into readable multi-line forms: extract deeply nested calls into named local variables, and split long method chains across multiple lines (following Prettier-style line-break conventions where reasonable).
reason: Deep nesting and long chained calls are difficult to scan, review, and maintain; named intermediates and line breaks clarify intent.
scope: JavaScript code, especially admin templates/scripts and complex expression chains
common_pattern: Complex JavaScript expressions—whether deeply nested calls or long method chains—should be decomposed into named local variables or broken across multiple lines for readability.

text: When working with `<template>` elements in Stimulus controllers, cache the template element reference itself and access its `.content` (DocumentFragment) only at the point of cloning. Clone the specific node needed by querying within `this.templatesTarget.content` rather than casting the target and cloning the whole content.
reason: Avoids repeated DOM queries, preserves access to element methods like `remove()` for later cleanup, and makes template selection simpler and more flexible (e.g., using optional chaining and early returns when a node is missing).
common_pattern: Best practices for handling `<template>.content` (a DocumentFragment) in Stimulus controllers: caching element references, selectively cloning nodes from template content, treating empty fragments as valid, and documenting non-obvious casts/clones.

text: In teardown/deactivate methods, clear timers directly with clearTimeout and avoid redundant cleanup: do not call clearTimeout inside the timer's own callback, do not set the timer field to undefined after clearTimeout, and do not rely on value-change callbacks (e.g., loadingValueChanged) that may not fire during disconnect.
reason: Timer callbacks only run after the timer has fired, making clearTimeout in the callback a no-op; clearTimeout is sufficient without resetting the timer field; and controller disconnect paths may not invoke value-change callbacks, so cleanup must happen directly.
common_pattern: Timer cleanup in deactivate/teardown should be direct and avoid redundant or ineffective cleanup steps, especially not relying on callbacks that may not fire during disconnect.

text: When constructing notifications or other event payloads that contain interpolated user-facing message text, assign the full message string to a named const before building the payload.
reason: Separates message content from event construction and makes notification code easier to read and maintain.
common_pattern: Message-string construction and formatting conventions for user/developer-facing output: isolate message text when building payloads, and write messages in a consistent, readable style.

text: When code selects between two alternatives based on configuration or a value (a method, a default, a returned variant), resolve the choice once — into a local variable, or by checking the non-default case first — and use that single resolution everywhere; avoid duplicating the same default or conditional expression across branches.
reason: Avoids duplicated branching logic and keeps the same default/selection value from being declared in multiple places, making behavior consistent and easier to maintain.
common_pattern: Simplification of conditional branching: single-source the selected branch/default instead of duplicating it across if/else arms, and choose the broadest applicable default for the API.

text: For multi-branch dispatch on a single value (e.g., a string mode or enum), use Python `match`/`case` structural pattern matching instead of long `if`/`elif` chains when the project's minimum supported Python version is 3.10+.
